# Dev.to vs Hashnode vs Medium vs your own blog: where should a developer actually write in 2026?
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/dev-to-vs-hashnode-vs-medium-for-developers/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## Where should a developer write in 2026: Dev.to, Hashnode or Medium?

**Your own domain first, for ownership and search equity; Dev.to second, for the fastest path to an engaged developer reader and a free posting API; Hashnode third, if you want a free custom-domain blog, though its API now sits behind a paid plan; Medium last, or not at all, because its paywall and algorithm work against an unknown technical writer. Publish on your own site, then syndicate to Dev.to with a canonical link back. That single habit captures most of the benefit of all four platforms.**


I publish across all of these plus my own site, and the pattern below is what actually moved readers and search rankings, not what each platform promises in its marketing [8][9].

> A platform can promote your post for a week. A domain you own compounds for years.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What is Dev.to, and who is it for?

**A community-run publishing platform for developers, built on the open-source Forem software, with tags, reactions, comments and a genuinely active audience of working developers [1]. Its posting API is free, which makes it the natural platform to auto-publish to alongside your own site. Discovery happens through tags and the community feed rather than search, so a Dev.to post's first burst of readers comes from people who follow the tag, not from Google, though good posts do get indexed and found later [2].**


## What is Hashnode, and what changed with its API?

**A blogging platform built specifically for developers, with a free custom domain from day one, clean themes, and good default SEO, which made it a favourite for a personal tech blog without hosting to manage [3]. As of 2026 its programmatic posting API sits behind a paid plan, which matters if your workflow is automated publishing rather than writing by hand in its editor; manual posting through the dashboard remains free. If you write by hand and want a free-domain blog, it is still a solid choice; if you automate, check current pricing before building on it.**



## What is Medium, and should I bother with it?

**A general publishing platform with a metered paywall, a recommendation algorithm, and the Partner Program for earning from reads [4]. For an unknown technical writer, both work against you: the paywall costs some readers a click, and the algorithm favours engagement patterns that generic, punchy writing produces more than technical depth. Medium can still work if you already have an audience elsewhere, or if you want a specific piece to reach non-developer readers a technical platform would not. As a default home for developer writing, it is not the strongest choice in 2026.**


## Why does my own domain matter more than any platform?

**Because search rankings, backlinks and reader trust accumulate on the domain the content lives on, and that domain is the one thing a platform cannot take from you, change the rules on, or shut down. A post on your own site under your name builds your search presence for years; the same words on a platform mostly build the platform's. Google's canonical URL system exists precisely so the same content can appear in several places while search credit flows to one chosen original [5]. Choose your own site as that original.**



## What is syndication, and how do I do it properly?

**Publish the full post on your own site first. Then post the same content, or a shortened version with a link, on Dev.to and Hashnode, setting the canonical URL field to your original where the platform supports it, which tells search engines your site is the source [5]. Wait a day or two before syndicating so your own site gets indexed first. This way each platform brings you readers who click through, while your domain keeps the search credit.**



## Which should I pick if I can only maintain one?

**Your own site if you can spare an afternoon to set it up on a free host, because everything else follows from having a home. If you genuinely cannot maintain a personal site yet, Dev.to alone, for the free API and the community, is the single best substitute, and you can add your own domain later without losing the posts, since they stay live on Dev.to regardless.**




## What mistakes do developers make with technical writing platforms?

**Writing only on Medium and wondering why nobody in the developer community sees it. Cross-posting without a canonical link and accidentally competing with your own original for search rankings. Building an automated pipeline around an API that then moves behind a paywall, without a fallback. Spreading across five platforms and maintaining none well. Never writing on a domain you control, so years of writing build someone else's audience instead of yours.**



## Where should I start?

**If you do not have a personal site yet, start there this week; if you do, publish your next post on it first and syndicate to Dev.to the same day.** For a session on building a writing habit that compounds into a career, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# Do you actually need a GPU for AI? A plain VRAM and hardware guide for students: what runs on a laptop, what needs to be rented, and what needs neither
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/do-you-need-a-gpu-for-ai-vram-and-hardware-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## Do I actually need a GPU for AI work?

**Usually not, for most of what a student does. Calling a model through an API, ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, needs no GPU at all; the provider's hardware does the generation, and your laptop only sends and receives text. The case that genuinely needs a GPU with real VRAM is running or fine-tuning an open-weight model locally, and even then, free cloud notebooks or an hourly rented GPU usually cover it without buying anything.**


Most of the production systems I run are API-first specifically to avoid this question entirely for the majority of the workload; the GPU question only comes up for the specific slice that touches an open model directly.

> Buy a GPU for the project that actually needs one, not for the fear that every AI project might.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What actually needs GPU memory, and what doesn't?

**Using a hosted model API: no GPU needed. Running a small open model locally for inference, chatting with a 7 to 8 billion parameter model through Ollama: modest VRAM, often fits on a good consumer GPU or even a strong CPU with patience. Fine-tuning a small to medium open model with LoRA or QLoRA: meaningful VRAM, but far less than full fine-tuning thanks to quantization [5]. Training a model from scratch: serious VRAM and usually multiple GPUs, essentially never a student's first project.**



## How much VRAM does a given model actually need?

**Roughly, for inference, a model needs about the number of parameters times the bytes per parameter: a 7 billion parameter model at 16-bit precision needs roughly 14 GB just to hold the weights, before accounting for the activation memory a request also uses. Quantizing to 8-bit roughly halves that, and to 4-bit roughly quarters it, which is why a model that needs 14 GB at full precision can often run in under 5 GB quantized [1][7]. Fine-tuning needs more on top of the base weights for gradients and optimiser state, which is exactly the memory pressure QLoRA was built to reduce [5].**



## What free options exist before I rent or buy anything?

**Google Colab's free tier gives a shared GPU with real, if variable, availability, enough for learning, small experiments, and light fine-tuning runs [2]. Kaggle offers free GPU and TPU hours on notebooks tied to your account, with a generous weekly quota [3]. Both are enough to complete most course exercises, small fine-tuning projects, and learning experiments without spending anything; the free tiers only become the bottleneck once a project needs sustained, guaranteed access or more memory than the free tier's GPU offers.**



## When should I rent a cloud GPU instead of using a free tier?

**When a task needs more VRAM or more sustained, guaranteed time than a free tier reliably offers, a bigger fine-tuning run, a longer training job, or repeated runs where waiting on shared free-tier availability costs more time than the rental costs money. Services that rent GPUs by the hour make this cheap for occasional use: a few hours of a mid-range GPU for a real fine-tuning experiment typically costs less than a two-week wait on an oversubscribed free tier [6].**



## When does buying a personal GPU actually make sense?

**When you run GPU-heavy work often enough that the cumulative cost of renting exceeds a GPU's price within a reasonable time, or when you specifically need a persistent local setup for reasons free and rented options do not cover, offline work, specific hardware experiments, or teaching others hands-on. For most students, this point arrives much later than the anxiety about needing a GPU does; do not buy hardware to solve a problem a free tier or an hour of rental already solves.**



## What mistakes do students make about GPU hardware?

**Assuming every AI project needs a GPU, when most API-based work needs none. Buying hardware before hitting an actual limit on free tiers. Ignoring quantization and assuming a model needs its full-precision memory footprint. Renting a much larger GPU than a quantized, LoRA-adapted fine-tuning run actually requires, paying for headroom nobody used. Never checking a model's actual memory footprint before assuming a task is impossible on the hardware already available.**


## GPU and hardware interview questions

**Explain what determines a model's memory footprint at inference time. Explain how quantization changes that footprint and its trade-offs. Describe when you would use an API instead of running a model locally. Explain the difference in memory needs between inference and fine-tuning. Describe how you would size a GPU rental for a specific fine-tuning job. The strongest answer includes a specific memory calculation you did for a real project.**



## Where should I start?

**Before assuming a project needs a GPU, check whether an API already covers it. If it genuinely needs a local model, try a quantized version on Colab's free tier first, and only look at renting once you hit a real limit.** For a hands-on session on right-sizing AI infrastructure for student budgets, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# FastAPI for AI applications: async endpoints for LLM calls, dependency injection, streaming responses, and the patterns that hold up in production
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/fastapi-for-ai-applications/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## Why is FastAPI the default choice for serving AI applications?

**Because an AI application spends most of its request time waiting on slow network calls, a model API, an embedding call, a vector database query, and FastAPI's async support means the server can handle other requests during that wait instead of blocking a whole worker thread on it [1][6]. Combined with automatic request validation from type hints, a built-in docs UI, and dependency injection for clean wiring of providers and settings, it removes most of the boilerplate a Flask-based service would need to hand-build for the same job.**


Both production systems I run day to day, a RAG platform and a document extraction service, are FastAPI applications underneath, and the async layer is not a nice-to-have, it is the difference between a server that serves five concurrent users and one that serves fifty on the same hardware [11][12].

> A synchronous web server serving LLM calls is a waiter who stands at one table until the kitchen finishes a dish, ignoring everyone else in the restaurant. Async is the waiter who takes the next order while the first dish cooks.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## How does async actually help when the model call is still slow?

**The model call itself is not made faster by async; a five-second generation still takes five seconds. What async changes is what the server does during that five seconds: instead of one worker thread sitting idle waiting for the response, `await`ing an async HTTP call to the model API frees that worker to handle other incoming requests, and resumes this one when the model's response arrives [6]. One process can then hold many concurrent slow requests in flight, which is exactly the shape of load an LLM-backed API sees.**



## What is the single most common FastAPI mistake in AI apps?

**Calling a synchronous client inside an `async def` route. If your model provider's SDK, or your database driver, does not itself support async and you call it directly inside an async route without offloading it, that call blocks the event loop exactly the way a fully synchronous server would, silently cancelling the whole benefit of using FastAPI. The fix is to use the provider's async client if one exists, or run the blocking call in a thread pool with `run_in_threadpool` so it does not block the event loop while it waits.**



## How does dependency injection fit into an AI application?

**FastAPI's dependency injection system is where the clean project structure of settings, providers, and database sessions actually gets wired into each incoming request [2]. A `get_settings()` dependency provides typed configuration; a `get_llm_client()` dependency provides the model provider instance; a `get_db_session()` dependency provides a database session scoped to the request and closed automatically afterward. Routes declare what they need as parameters, and FastAPI resolves and injects them, which keeps route functions thin and makes swapping a provider or a database a change in one place, not a search-and-replace across the codebase.**




## How do I stream LLM responses token by token?

**Return a `StreamingResponse` whose body is an async generator that yields chunks as they arrive from the model provider's streaming API, rather than collecting the full response before returning anything [4]. Most model providers expose a streaming mode over server-sent events specifically for this [5]. The user sees the answer appear progressively, which cuts perceived latency dramatically even though total generation time is unchanged, because the wait for the first token is far shorter than the wait for the whole answer.**



## When do I need background tasks versus a real task queue?

**FastAPI's built-in `BackgroundTasks` is for quick, fire-and-forget work tied to a single request's lifecycle, sending a notification email after a response is returned, with no need to track its status or retry it [3]. A real task queue, Celery or an equivalent, is for anything that needs retries, scheduling, monitoring, or to survive the web server restarting, a long document-processing job, a nightly re-embedding run, a batch of API calls that must complete even if the request that triggered them is long gone [8]. Reaching for background tasks when you actually need a queue is how "fire and forget" jobs quietly disappear when the server restarts mid-job.**



## What does a clean FastAPI layer for an AI app look like?

**Routes stay thin: parse the request, resolve dependencies, call into the application's core logic, return a response, ideally streamed. All the actual work, retrieval, generation, validation, sits in the modules described in a proper project structure, not inline in the route function [10]. Settings come from dependency injection, never read directly from the environment inside a route. Errors from the model provider are caught and translated into clean HTTP error responses, not leaked as raw provider exceptions.**



## FastAPI interview questions for AI roles

**Explain why async matters specifically for LLM-backed APIs. Describe how dependency injection would wire a swappable model provider. Explain how you would stream a model's response to a frontend. Compare BackgroundTasks with a real task queue and say when each applies. Describe the most common way a FastAPI app silently loses its async benefits. The strongest answer includes a concurrency bug you found and fixed, not just the theory.**



## Where should I start?

**Take an existing script that calls a model API and wrap it in a FastAPI route with a streaming response and one dependency for the client. An evening turns a script into a real, concurrent-capable service.** For a hands-on session on serving AI applications with FastAPI, from a script to production, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.


---

# Free AI tools every CS student should learn in 2026: coding assistants, models, notebooks, deployment and the ones I built, with no signup
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/free-ai-tools-for-students/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## Which AI tools should a CS student learn first?

**Five categories, in this order: a coding assistant in your editor, so you build faster; a way to call a model, a free API tier or a local runner; a notebook with a free GPU, for experiments and fine-tuning; a database with a free tier, so projects have real persistence; and a platform to deploy on, so projects have a URL. Everything else is optional until a project demands it. Learn each by shipping something with it, not by watching a tutorial about it.**


I mentor 200-plus students through TechVerse Enclave and the same question arrives weekly: which tools? The list below is what I actually use and what students who finish projects actually use, with the free-tier limits that matter. Because signup friction stops more students than difficulty does, I also built fifteen tools that need no account at all, at tools.scult.in [15].

> A tool you have to sign up for is a tool you try tomorrow. A tool that opens in a tab is a tool you use now. That is the whole reason tools.scult.in exists.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## Which coding assistant should students use?

**One you can afford and that lives in your editor. GitHub Copilot is free for verified students through the Student Developer Pack and works inside VS Code [5][6]. Cursor is an AI-first editor with a free tier [13]. Claude Code runs an agent in your terminal that can read, edit and run your project [14]. Pick one, learn its limits, and use it for boilerplate, tests, refactors and explanations of unfamiliar code. Turn it off when you are learning a fundamental for the first time, or you will not learn it.**



The rule I give mentees: assistants make you faster at what you understand and slower at learning what you do not. Write your first RAG pipeline by hand; use the assistant for the tenth.

## How do students get free access to LLMs?

**Three ways. Free API tiers: Google AI Studio gives Gemini API access with a free quota [10]; Groq offers fast inference on open models with a free tier [11]; OpenRouter routes to many models, some free [12]. Local models: Ollama runs open-weight models on your laptop with no account and no cost [4]. Hosted playgrounds: Hugging Face hosts thousands of models and free courses [3]. Start with a free API for speed, and Ollama for privacy and unlimited experimentation.**



Free tiers change often; the pricing pages are the truth and this table is a map [10][11][12].

## Where can students get free GPUs?

**Google Colab gives free GPU sessions with time and availability limits, enough for QLoRA on a small model [1]. Kaggle Notebooks give weekly GPU hours with a generous quota, and host datasets you can use directly [2]. Hugging Face Spaces can run demos with optional paid GPU [3]. For learning: fine-tune a 1 to 3B model on Colab, then move to Kaggle when you need longer runs. Save checkpoints to Drive or the Hub because sessions end.**


## Which databases and backends have free tiers good enough for projects?

**Supabase gives hosted Postgres with auth, storage and the pgvector extension on a free tier, which is a complete backend for a RAG project [7]. Firebase and MongoDB Atlas have free tiers too. For deploying a Python API, Railway and Render both offer free or trial tiers that sleep when idle [8][9]. GitHub Pages hosts static front ends for free, including this site. The pattern: one Postgres, one API host, one static host, all free until you have users.**




## What free tools did you build, and why no signup?

**Fifteen browser tools at tools.scult.in, a 1,211-prompt library where every prompt is stamped with the model and date it was tested against, a 50,000-plus agent-skills library, and a public MCP server so agents can call the same tools [15]. Thirteen of the fifteen tools never send a byte to a server; they run entirely in your browser, which is both faster and the simplest privacy story there is [17]. No signup because every signup screen is a place where a student decides to do it later.**



Every calculator shows its formula so you can check it rather than trust it, and the prompt library's stamps exist because a prompt that worked on one model version is a hypothesis on the next.

## How should students use AI tools without hurting their learning?

**Decide before each task whether the goal is output or understanding. For output, a deadline, a boilerplate, a refactor, use the assistant fully and review what it wrote. For understanding, a new algorithm, a first pipeline, a concept for an exam, write it yourself first, then ask the assistant to critique it. Never submit code you cannot explain line by line, because the interview will ask you to. The students who do best treat assistants like a senior colleague: consult often, copy never without reading.**



## Which AI tools help with research, writing and productivity?

**For reading papers: a chat model with the PDF, asking for the method and the limitations, then reading the paper anyway. For writing: an assistant for structure and clarity, never for facts you have not checked. For notes: any tool that exports plain text, so your notes outlive the tool. For search: AI answer engines for orientation, primary sources for anything you will cite. The habit that matters is checking the source, which no tool does for you.**


## What free AI tools are there for design and content?

**For diagrams and slides, most design tools now have free AI features; for images, be careful with licences and never present generated images as photographs of real events. For content, the same rule as writing: structure from the model, facts from sources. The colour palette generator and favicon generator at tools.scult.in cover the two design tasks every student project actually needs, with contrast checks built in [15].**



## Which tools will still matter in five years?

**None of the specific ones, probably, and all of the skills: prompting a model precisely, evaluating its output, deploying a service, reading documentation, reading a paper, and knowing when to switch the assistant off. Learn tools as instances of those skills, and the next tool is an afternoon, not a semester. My longer list with the reasoning is on the portfolio [16].**




## Where should I start today?

**Open tools.scult.in, use one tool, copy one stamped prompt into your assistant, and ship one page to GitHub Pages before you sleep.** For a hands-on session at your college that ends with every student having a deployed project built with free tools, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# From a BCA in Kanpur to GenAI engineer: how I got here, what actually mattered, and what I would tell my first-year self
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/from-bca-student-to-genai-engineer/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## Can you become a GenAI engineer from a BCA at a college nobody has heard of?

**Yes. I did a Bachelor of Computer Applications at Dr. Virendra Swarup Institute of Computer Studies in Kanpur, 2023 to 2026, and by the first half of 2026 I had shipped five production AI systems as a GenAI engineer and was leading engineering for a 14-member team at SCULT INDIA. Not one interview that mattered asked about the college. Every one asked about what I had built and what broke. This page is the path, without the parts that make it sound inevitable.**


The full resume with dates is on the portfolio [1]. What follows is the version with the decisions in it.

> The certificate says BCA, Kanpur. The GitHub says five production AI apps, three first prizes, a 14-member team. Recruiters read the second document first when you give them a reason to.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What did the first year look like?

**Foundations, and a community that did not exist yet. In 2023 I started the BCA and started TechVerse Enclave, a developer community that began as a place for a few of us to learn web development together and became, over three years, a 500-plus member community where I have mentored more than 200 students. The first year was Python, JavaScript, Git, one deployed page, and the habit of teaching what I had learned the week before.**



That roadmap is the one I gave 100+ first-years at the VSICS induction in July 2025, because it is the one that worked, not the one that sounds impressive [8].

## How did the community change things?

**More than anything else. TechVerse Enclave started as a hackathon team and a group chat and became the place where I learned to teach, to organise, to run sessions and to be known for something. Mentoring 200 students meant answering the same questions until I understood them properly. The sessions I ran inside the community became the sessions colleges invited me to give. The people in it became teammates, clients and referrals. Every later opportunity traces back to it.**


The story of the first 500 members, with what worked and what did not, is written up separately [4]. The short version: the community did not grow because I promoted it; it grew because sessions happened every week whether five people or fifty showed up.

## What did hackathons teach that classes did not?

**Scope, demos and losing. Three first prizes: Changethon 2025 at the National Social Summit, IIT Roorkee, with KrishGyan, voice-first farming advice over WhatsApp; Product Genesis at Vividhotsava 2025, CSJMU Kanpur, with BrandHive; and BYTEBATTLE by MeetKats, with Annapurna, surplus food coordination. A top-three at IIT Kanpur. And STROT, which we did not win, because we built more and explained less than the team that did. The loss is the one I quote most in talks.**



Everything I now teach about hackathon strategy comes from those four rooms [5].

## How did the first clients and SCULT INDIA happen?

**Through the community and through shipping small things well. SCULT INDIA is an AI-first software agency; from 2024 I led engineering for it, architecture, UI/UX, deployment and delivery for a 14-member cross-functional team, and designed SCULT Studio CRM, the internal platform that runs projects, clients and operations [9]. The client products came one at a time, a pest-control business site in Goa, a music label, a digital library, a media company, and each one taught delivery under a deadline, which no college project can.**


Leading fourteen people while still a student is its own story, mostly about saying no and writing things down [6].


## How did the GenAI role come, and what did it produce?

**From the portfolio. NextUpgrad Web Solutions hired me as a GenAI engineer for February to July 2026 on the strength of shipped systems, and in those six months I independently designed, built and shipped five production AI applications: RAG.NextUpgrad, a retrieval platform with hybrid search, reranking, streaming citations and a confidence gate; FineTune Studio, a QLoRA fine-tuning platform with live telemetry; DocuLens AI, schema-validated document extraction with deterministic compliance scoring; FaceVision, browser-only face recognition and liveness that stores embeddings, never images; and the OCR & Speech Workspace, page-batched OCR, live speech-to-text and document chat with page citations. All with Docker, CI/CD, structured logging and metrics [1][10].**


Six months, five systems, because the habits, shipping weekly, testing, writing READMEs, evaluating honestly, were already three years old. The role did not create the habits. The habits created the role.

## What actually mattered, in order?

**Shipping small things every week. A community to learn and teach inside. Hackathons for scope and demos. Real clients for delivery. Writing in public so people could find the work. Reading the papers that mattered with a notebook open. Saying yes to every session and judging invitation early. Applying before I felt ready. Not: the college's name, certificates, or waiting for a placement cell.**



## What would I tell my first-year self?

**Start the community in month one, not month six. Post the first project even though it is embarrassing; the embarrassment is the point. Go to the hackathon two hours away. Learn to write a README before learning a fourth framework. Talk to the strangers at events. Ask for the client work. Read the papers, they are shorter than the tutorials. And stop comparing your college to the ones with placement cells; compare your GitHub to theirs.**


The longer letter is on the portfolio [8]. Most of it is the list above, said more gently.

## Was it worth it, and what is next?

**Yes. The year of shipping, 2025 into 2026, produced the systems, the team and the sessions, and it produced this site: a hundred pages answering the questions students and engineers actually search, written from what I built [7]. Next is more of the same at a larger scale: GenAI roles and products, more campuses, more judging panels, and a community that outgrows me. If you are in a first-year seat in a college nobody has heard of, the path is open, and the first step is a project this week.**





## Talk to me

**If you are at a college like mine and want the path explained in person, that is one of the sessions I give, free for student communities.** Email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite. The projects are all public at github.com/Pranjulrathour [10].

# GenAI and LLM interview questions with answers: RAG, fine-tuning, prompting, agents, evaluation and system design, from both sides of the table
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/genai-interview-questions/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What do GenAI engineer interviews actually ask?

**Six things, in some order: LLM fundamentals, tokens, context, attention, hallucination; RAG, how you build and evaluate retrieval; fine-tuning, when and how with LoRA; prompting and agents, including safety; evaluation and cost, how you know it works and what it costs; and one system design where you assemble the pieces. Plus a walkthrough of a project you built, which is where most decisions get made. Definitions get you past the first minute. Trade-offs and stories get you the offer.**


I have sat on both sides: interviewing candidates for SCULT INDIA and being interviewed for GenAI roles. The pattern is consistent enough that this page is the preparation I now give mentees, with the answers I would want to hear. Longer notes are on the portfolio [11][12].

> The question is never really "what is RAG". The question is "have you built one, and do you know what broke". Answer the second question every time.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## LLM fundamentals: what will they ask?

**Expect: what is a token and why does it matter for cost; what is the context window and one failure mode of long contexts; explain attention in one minute; what is hallucination and how do you manage it; open-weight versus API models for a given product; what is the difference between a base model and an instruct model. Answer each with the concept in one sentence, then a consequence for a product you built.**



## RAG interview questions

**Expect: explain RAG end to end; why is chunking important and how do you choose a size; why add keyword search to embeddings; what does a reranker do; how do you evaluate retrieval separately from generation; how do you stop the model answering when the documents do not contain the answer; how would you handle multi-tenant documents. Every question maps to a stage of the pipeline; know the pipeline and you know the questions.**



The paper to cite is Lewis et al. [1]; the metric framework most interviewers know is RAGAS [7]. The answer that separates candidates is to the evaluation question: "I measure retrieval recall on twenty labelled questions before I look at a single generated answer, because a system can be faithful to the wrong passage."

## Fine-tuning interview questions

**Expect: when would you fine-tune instead of using RAG; explain LoRA and QLoRA; how do you prepare a dataset; how do you read a loss curve; what is catastrophic forgetting; how do you evaluate a fine-tuned model honestly; can you fine-tune GPT. The trap question is "how would you teach the model our product facts", and the right answer is "I would not, I would retrieve them, and fine-tune only for the voice and format".**



## Prompt engineering and agent interview questions

**Expect: system prompt versus user prompt and why the split matters for security; what is prompt injection and how do you limit its damage; when does chain-of-thought help and when does it waste tokens; how do you test a prompt; what is an agent and where does the model's judgement actually belong; how would you stop an agent taking a harmful action; when is a workflow better than an agent. Safety questions are where candidates who have only prototyped get exposed.**


The references interviewers respect: chain-of-thought [5], ReAct for agents [6], OWASP for security [9], and Anthropic's guide for the workflow-versus-agent distinction [10]. The answer to "how do you stop a harmful action" is not a clever prompt; it is least-privilege tools and a human confirmation for anything irreversible.


## Evaluation and cost questions

**Expect: how do you know your system works; what metrics do you track; how do you test a prompt change before deploying; how much does this feature cost per month; how would you cut that cost in half; what do you log. The interviewer is testing whether you treat an LLM system like software. Answer with a fixed evaluation set, metrics per stage, a CI check, tokens logged per request, and a cost model: input plus output tokens times price times requests.**



## System design questions for GenAI roles

**Expect one design in 30 to 45 minutes: a support chatbot over company documents, a document extraction service, a coding assistant, a voice assistant for a regional language. Structure it: clarify users and constraints, draw the request path, name each component and its failure mode, say what you would measure, estimate cost, and state what you would cut for version one. Interviewers grade the trade-offs you name unprompted, not the boxes you draw.**



## Behavioural and project questions

**Expect: tell me about a project; what broke and what did you do; a time you disagreed with a technical decision; how you handle a requirement you think is wrong; why this role. For the project question, use one project and go deep: the problem, the decision you made, the failure you hit, the fix, the measured result. My RAG platform's confidence gate exists because of a failure; that story has done more for me in interviews than any definition.**


My separate note on the "tell me about a project" question, with the structure and a worked example, is on the portfolio [13].

## Coding rounds for GenAI roles

**Expect Python: parse and validate a JSON output against a schema; implement reciprocal rank fusion over two ranked lists; write a retry with backoff around an API call; chunk a text by paragraphs with a size cap; compute cosine similarity; write a small evaluation loop. Rarely leetcode-style puzzles. Write clear, typed, tested code, talk while you write, and handle the edge case out loud. The interviewer is watching how you work, not whether you finish.**


```python
def reciprocal_rank_fusion(*ranked_lists: list[str], k: int = 60) -> list[str]:
    """Fuse ranked lists of ids; 1/(k+rank) per list, summed. A common coding-round question."""
    scores: dict[str, float] = {}
    for ranked in ranked_lists:
        for rank, doc_id in enumerate(ranked, start=1):
            scores[doc_id] = scores.get(doc_id, 0.0) + 1.0 / (k + rank)
    return sorted(scores, key=scores.get, reverse=True)
```

## How should freshers prepare for a GenAI interview?

**Build one RAG project and one fine-tune before the interview, so every answer has a story. Read four papers: transformer, RAG, LoRA, QLoRA. Write the evaluation set for your project, because the evaluation question is where freshers lose. Rehearse the project walkthrough with a timer, failure by failure. Prepare three questions to ask about how the team evaluates and ships. Then be honest about what you have not done; the sentence "I have not done that, here is how I would start" gets hired.**



## Questions to ask the interviewer

**How do you evaluate model changes before they ship? What does your logging show for a bad answer? How often do requirements change and how do you handle it? Who owns prompt versions? What was the last production incident and what changed after? These tell you whether the team treats LLM systems as engineering, and they tell the interviewer you do.**



## Want a mock interview or a session for your batch?

**I run GenAI interview preparation sessions for final-year batches and tech clubs, with a live system design and a project walkthrough clinic.** Email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# Hackathon judging criteria and a rubric organisers can copy: how judges score, how to brief a panel, how to break ties, and how to judge fairly in 15 minutes per team
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/hackathon-judging-criteria-and-rubric/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What are the judging criteria for a hackathon?

**Four things, whatever the rubric calls them: feasibility, does it work and could it exist; innovation, is there a real insight, not a new coat of paint; practicality, would the stated user actually adopt it; and problem solving, did the team understand the problem before building. Presentation and teamwork are usually smaller weights. Organisers dress these up with different names; judges who have sat on panels recognise the same four underneath.**


These four are the ones I put on the screen when I brief a judging room, because I learned them from the other side: three first prizes, one loss, and then panels of my own [1][2]. The full rubric with score anchors is on the portfolio and free to copy.

> Judges do not score the idea. They score the evidence: what ran, what the team understood, what they cut. Write the rubric so it can only be filled in from evidence.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## A rubric you can copy

**Five criteria, weights that sum to one hundred, and score anchors at 2, 5 and 8 out of 10 so every judge means the same thing by a 7.**



Weights are a choice; my reasoning for putting feasibility and problem solving above innovation is that innovation is the easiest criterion to fake with words and the hardest to verify in three minutes [4]. For an AI hackathon, add one line under feasibility: is the model doing real work on real inputs, or is the AI a label on a rules engine?

## How should a judge spend the time per team?

**Fifteen minutes: three for the pitch, two for the demo if it was not live, five for questions, two to score alone, three to confer if the panel scores together. Judge the demo and the answers, not the deck. Ask at least one question that tests understanding rather than the project. Score independently before discussing, then discuss only where scores differ by more than two points.**



## What questions should judges ask?

**Who is this for, and have you spoken to them? What happens when it fails? What did you build yourselves versus take from a library? Why did you cut what you cut? What would you do with a month? How is this different from the existing solution? What did you learn that surprised you? The first and last reveal problem understanding; the middle ones reveal feasibility and judgement.**



## How do I brief a judging panel?

**Fifteen minutes before the first pitch, all judges in one room. Cover: the four criteria and their weights, the score anchors with one example each, the time protocol and who keeps time, the rule of independent scoring before discussion, conflicts of interest and how to declare them, tie-breaking, and how feedback is delivered. Hand each judge a one-page sheet per team. Ask them to score the demo they saw, not the potential they imagine.**


My briefing outline, which takes exactly fifteen minutes, is written up separately [3]. The two things new judges most need to hear: score independently first, and a working small thing beats a described big thing.


## How do you break ties and handle conflicts of interest?

**Decide both before the event and write them down. Tie-break by a pre-declared criterion, usually feasibility, then problem solving, then a short re-demo if still tied; never by adding a new criterion in the room. Conflicts: any judge who has mentored a team, knows a member personally, or works for a sponsor whose product the team used declares it and abstains from scoring that team; the remaining judges' scores are normalised. Publish both rules to teams with the criteria.**


Both processes, with the edge cases I have met, are written up in detail [5][6]. The commonest conflict at college hackathons is a mentor judging their own mentees, and the fix is simply to separate the two roles before the event.

## How should judges give feedback?

**One specific, actionable sentence per team, delivered privately or in writing, that names what would have moved the score: "the demo depended on Wi-Fi; seed the data next time", "you never named the user; start there". Not a ranking, not a critique of the idea, not encouragement without content. Teams remember one clear sentence for years, and it is the only part of judging that improves the next hackathon.**


My notes on feedback that actually helped teams, and the kind that did not, are on the portfolio [7].

## How do the criteria differ for Smart India Hackathon or corporate hackathons?

**The four criteria hold; the weights and a fifth item shift. Smart India Hackathon panels include the problem statement's owners, so fit with existing systems and policy carries extra weight, and the current year's official rubric governs [10]. Corporate hackathons weight practicality toward the sponsor's platform or data. Community events such as those run under Major League Hacking publish organiser guidance that leans toward learning and inclusion [9]. Read the event's own rubric, then map it onto the four.**



## How do I become a hackathon judge?

**Build and ship something first, then attend, then mentor, then ask the organiser for a panel seat. Organisers want judges who have shipped, can follow a rubric, show up on time and write feedback. After the first panel, invitations arrive with speaking invitations. Publish your rubric; organisers copy it and remember where it came from, which is how this one travels.**


My own path from participant to judge, and what organisers told me they look for, is written up separately [8].



## Need a judge, or a briefing for your panel?

**I judge and mentor at college hackathons and internal Smart India Hackathon rounds, on-site across India or remote, and I brief panels using the rubric above. Free for student communities.** Send the date, format and problem statements to pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.



---

# Hackathon pitch deck template: the seven slides, the three-minute script, demo rules and what judges score, from three first prizes and the judging table
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/hackathon-pitch-deck-template/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What should a hackathon pitch deck contain?

**Seven slides in this order: the problem in the user's words; the user and what the problem costs them; the live demo, which is not a slide but a switch to your app; how it works, one diagram; what you cut and why; what is next and what you need; the team with roles and contact details. Three minutes total, with about ninety seconds on the demo. Anything else, a market size, a competitor grid, a technology logo wall, comes out.**


I have pitched from the floor three times for a first prize and once for a loss I still learn from, and I have sat on the other side scoring decks with a timer running [7][8]. The structure below is what wins from both seats. The downloadable version and the reasoning behind each slide are on the portfolio [1].

> The judges have seen twenty decks today. They will remember one demo and one sentence. Build the deck to deliver exactly those two things.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What goes on each slide?

**One idea per slide, readable from the back of the room, with the words you will say, not paragraphs you will read. Here is each slide with its job and its time.**



The "what we cut" slide surprises teams, and it is the slide that has most often earned a nod from judges I have sat beside. It says: we understood the problem well enough to know what was not the problem.

## How do I structure a three-minute hackathon pitch?

**Thirty seconds of setup, ninety of demo, sixty of close. Setup: the user, the pain, and the one-line solution. Demo: the happy path, narrated in the user's terms, "Priya uploads her invoice, and here is the total, validated". Close: how it works, what you cut, what is next, the ask. Rehearse with a timer three times. If you run over in rehearsal, cut the setup, never the demo.**



### What is a good opening line for a hackathon pitch?

**The user's name and their problem, in ten words. "Ramesh grows wheat near Kanpur and cannot read the advisory SMS." Not "Hi, we are Team Innovators and we built an AI-powered platform." The first sentence decides whether the judge listens to the second. My two-minute pitch notes cover the opening in detail [2][5].**


## How do I demo without it crashing?

**Freeze the code two hours before. Seed the data so no step depends on a live third-party call or the venue Wi-Fi. Rehearse the exact click path three times on the machine and browser you will present from. Record a full-path video and keep it open in a tab. Assign one person to drive and one to talk. If it breaks anyway, switch to the video without apology and keep narrating; judges score recovery too.**



Our loss at STROT came from a live API call over venue Wi-Fi [8]. My technical checklist for demos that survive is written up separately [3], and every team I mentor gets it before the event.


## What do judges score, and how does the deck serve it?

**Four things: feasibility, innovation, practicality and problem solving, with presentation as a smaller weight. The demo proves feasibility. The problem and user slides prove problem solving and practicality. The how-it-works slide and the "what we cut" slide show innovation and judgement. The close shows you know what a next step is. If a slide does not serve one of those four, remove it.**



## How do I handle Q&A after the pitch?

**Repeat the question aloud, answer the fair part in two sentences, and stop. Expect: who is this for and have you spoken to them; what happens when it fails; how is this different from the existing tool; what did you build versus borrow; what would you do with a month. Say "we did not get to that" when true. Judges test whether you understand your own project, and a short honest answer beats a long confident one every time.**


The full list of questions I have heard and asked, with the answers that landed, is on the portfolio [4].

## How do I adapt the deck for Smart India Hackathon?

**Use the template the portal prescribes for that year exactly, because reviewers check for it [6]. Inside it, keep the same order: the department's problem in its vocabulary, the demo or a video of it, one diagram, feasibility and the constraints you honoured, impact for the department and the citizen, and a pilot plan. Replace "the ask" with "how this runs inside the department next month". Ministry judges reward fit with existing systems more than novelty.**


## What mistakes lose pitches?

**Opening with the team and the stack. A slide of technology logos. Reading paragraphs off the screen. Explaining the architecture before showing the product. A demo that depends on Wi-Fi. Running over time so the demo gets cut. Ending with "thank you" instead of an ask. Five people speaking in turn with no handoff. Every one of these is on the checklists above, and every one I have watched sink a good build.**



## Do I need a video, a one-pager or a repository too?

**Yes to all three, and they take an hour. A two-minute screen recording of the demo for organisers and for your LinkedIn post. A one-page PDF with the problem, the solution, the diagram and the team, for judges who want to remember you. A repository with a README that states the problem, how to run it, and what you would do next. These outlast the event; the deck does not.**



## Can you review our deck before the hackathon?

**If your college or club is preparing teams for a hackathon, I run pitch clinics: each team presents for three minutes, gets scored on the rubric, and revises on the spot.** On-site across India or remote, free for student communities. Email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.



---

# Hackathon project ideas that win: 40 AI and software ideas for students, with the hard part of each, from three first prizes
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/hackathon-project-ideas/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What makes a hackathon project idea good?

**A good hackathon idea has four properties: a named user with a real friction, a before-and-after a judge can see in one demo, a hard technical part your team can finish in the time available, and a plausible next step after the event. Ambition is not one of the four. Every first prize I have won came from a smaller idea than the teams we beat, executed completely.**


KrishGyan won Changethon at IIT Roorkee because the demo was a farmer's voice note going in and spoken advice coming out, in the farmer's language, on WhatsApp, with no reading required [1]. Annapurna won BYTEBATTLE because a judge could watch one meal move from a hotel kitchen to a shelter through four clear roles [2]. BrandHive won Product Genesis because we showed the whole loop for a small business, not a features slide [3]. None of those ideas was novel. All of them were complete.

> Judges do not remember the idea. They remember the moment the demo worked and they understood who it was for.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## How do I generate hackathon ideas fast?

**Use a three-column frame: an audience, a friction, and what technology removes it. Audiences: farmers, first-year students, small shopkeepers, clinic staff, college offices, delivery workers, parents. Frictions: a form, a queue, a language barrier, a lost document, a phone call nobody answers, a spreadsheet updated by hand. Technology: voice in and out, document extraction, a RAG assistant over one set of documents, a vision check, an agent that finishes one repetitive task. Combine any row from each column and you have a candidate in thirty seconds.**



## 40 hackathon project ideas, with the hard part named

**Each idea below states the user, the demo and the hard part. Change the audience to match your problem statement; the shape carries over.**


### AI and generative AI

1. **Voice-first advisory over WhatsApp** for farmers or shopkeepers: voice note in, spoken answer out, in a regional language. Hard part: speech recognition quality on real audio. KrishGyan is this idea [1].
2. **RAG assistant over one college's documents**, syllabus, notices, previous-year papers, with page citations. Hard part: chunking messy PDFs so retrieval works.
3. **Invoice or receipt extraction to a spreadsheet** with validation that totals add up. Hard part: deterministic validation after the model extracts.
4. **Prescription reader** that turns a photo into a medication schedule with reminders. Hard part: handwriting and drug-name normalisation; keep a human confirm step.
5. **Lecture recording to notes**: transcribe, segment by topic, produce a summary and a quiz. Hard part: speaker diarisation and long-audio chunking.
6. **Resume to job-fit report** for a specific posting, with the gaps and one project suggestion per gap. Hard part: avoiding generic output; ground it in the posting text.
7. **Government scheme eligibility checker** by conversation: answer five questions, get the schemes you qualify for with the documents needed. Hard part: keeping the rules table accurate and cited.
8. **Code review agent for student repositories** that comments on a pull request with tests it ran. Hard part: sandboxing and a tight tool set.
9. **Local-language news summariser** for one district, from public feeds, with source links. Hard part: dedup across sources and honest attribution.
10. **Meeting-minutes agent** that joins a call recording, extracts decisions and owners, and files them. Hard part: precision on who owns what.

### Agriculture and rural

11. **Crop disease photo triage** with a confidence threshold and a "see an expert" path. Hard part: a model that admits uncertainty on out-of-distribution photos.
12. **Mandi price alerts by voice** for a crop and district. Hard part: reliable public price data ingestion.
13. **Irrigation scheduling from weather and soil inputs** with SMS output. Hard part: an honest, simple model rather than a fake precise one.
14. **Cold-storage or transport sharing** between small farmers. Hard part: the matching logic and trust; roles, as in Annapurna [2].
15. **Fertiliser dose calculator in a regional language**, offline-first. Hard part: getting the agronomy right and citing it.

### Education and campus

16. **Attendance by face recognition with liveness**, embeddings-only storage, per-class galleries. Hard part: threshold tuning and privacy design.
17. **Doubt-solving queue** for a class, with an LLM first pass and a teacher escalation. Hard part: knowing when the model should not answer.
18. **Placement tracker** that scrapes the college's notices and turns them into a calendar with deadlines. Hard part: parsing inconsistent notice formats.
19. **Lab equipment booking** with conflict detection and a waitlist. Hard part: none technical, which is why it ships.
20. **Peer tutoring marketplace** inside one campus, with verified student profiles. Hard part: trust and moderation.
21. **Exam paper generator from a syllabus** with difficulty tags and an answer key, reviewed by a teacher. Hard part: quality control and avoiding hallucinated facts.
22. **Accessibility reader** for scanned course PDFs: OCR to clean text to audio. Hard part: reading order on two-column pages.

### Health and public services

23. **Clinic queue and token system** with SMS updates for a primary health centre. Hard part: works on feature phones.
24. **Vaccination or check-up reminders** for a ward, by voice call in the local language. Hard part: opt-in, consent and unsubscribe from the first version.
25. **Blood donor coordination** with availability and distance, verified by a hospital contact. Hard part: verification without friction.
26. **Medical report explainer**: upload a lab report, get plain-language explanations of each line with the normal range cited, and a clear "ask your doctor" boundary. Hard part: restraint.
27. **Emergency contact card by QR** for two-wheeler riders. Hard part: none; the demo is the product.

### Fintech and small business

28. **GST invoice generator for a kirana shop** that works offline and syncs later. Hard part: offline-first data model.
29. **UPI QR with payment tracking for stalls and events**. Hard part: reconciliation.
30. **Expense splitting for hostels** with recurring bills and settlement suggestions. Hard part: none; polish wins.
31. **Loan document checklist assistant** that tells a first-time applicant what is missing from their file. Hard part: accurate, cited requirements.
32. **Small-business review responder** that drafts replies to Google reviews in the owner's voice, with approval before posting. Hard part: never auto-post.

### Civic, community and sustainability

33. **Surplus food coordination** between donors, NGOs and volunteers with verified impact. Hard part: roles and trust; this is Annapurna [2][7].
34. **Pothole and streetlight reporting** with photo, location and a public status board. Hard part: dedup of the same issue reported twice.
35. **Lost-and-found for a campus or a city event** with image matching. Hard part: matching without false positives.
36. **E-waste pickup scheduler** for a locality with a route for the collector. Hard part: route optimisation, kept simple.
37. **Water tanker demand aggregation** for a colony. Hard part: coordination logic and notifications.

### Developer tools and productivity

38. **One-click deploy of a student's Python project to a free host** with a generated README and Dockerfile. Hard part: handling the ten ways student projects are structured.
39. **Hackathon team finder** matching skills and availability inside one event. Hard part: cold start; seed it with the event's registrations.
40. **Prompt library with version stamps** per model and date, so a team knows which prompt worked where. Hard part: the discipline; I run one at tools.scult.in.

## Which ideas suit an AI hackathon specifically?

**The ones where the model does one narrow job with real inputs and a visible output: voice in and voice out, a photo to a structured record, a document set to cited answers, a repository to a review with evidence. Ideas 1 to 10 above are built for that. Avoid "a chatbot for X" unless X is a specific document set and the demo shows a citation; judges have seen a thousand generic chatbots.**



Open models make most of these feasible on a laptop: Whisper for speech [8], Ollama for a local LLM [9], and the Hugging Face hub for vision and embedding models [10].


## How do I adapt an idea to a Smart India Hackathon problem statement?

**Read the problem statement for its owner and its constraint. A ministry statement wants scale, compliance and integration with existing systems, so the idea should show a pilot that could grow and a data-handling story. A company statement wants one feature demonstrated on their kind of data. Map one idea from the list to the statement, then rewrite the user and the demo in the statement's own vocabulary. Never present a generic project with the statement's name pasted on.**


The official portal publishes each cycle's problem statements and rules, and they change every year, so read the current list before choosing [5]. The internal college round is where most teams are eliminated; treat that presentation as the final.

## What hackathon ideas work for beginners?

**Ideas 19, 27, 30 and 34: a booking system, an emergency QR card, an expense splitter, a reporting board. None needs a model, a dataset or an API key. Each can be finished, polished and demoed by a team learning as they go, and a finished beginner project beats an unfinished ambitious one on every rubric I have used. Add one small AI feature only if the core works by hour 20.**


## What ideas should I avoid?

**Anything that needs a dataset you do not have on day one. Anything whose demo depends on a third party approving an API key during the event. Anything with "blockchain" attached to a problem that a database solves. Anything that requires convincing a judge of a market instead of showing a user. Anything so broad that your three-minute demo would need ten. Novelty is not on the rubric; completeness is.**



## How do I present a hackathon idea?

**Lead with the user and the pain, in one sentence. Show the demo before you explain the architecture. Put one diagram of how it works. Say what you cut and why, which shows judgement. End with what you would build next and what you need. Three minutes, rehearsed three times. The idea gets thirty seconds; the demo gets ninety.**



## Can you help our team with an idea?

**If your college or hackathon wants a session on idea selection, scoping and demos before the event, or a judge or mentor during it, that is one of the things I do.** The longer list with 2026-specific angles is on the portfolio [4]. Email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# How does face recognition work? Detection, embeddings, thresholds and liveness, from building FaceVision
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-does-face-recognition-work/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## How does face recognition work?

**Face recognition works in four steps. A detector finds each face in the image and its landmarks. The face is aligned and cropped to a standard size. A recognition network turns the crop into an embedding, a vector of a few hundred numbers in which faces of the same person land close together. Finally the system compares that embedding with stored ones and declares a match when the distance falls under a threshold. Everything else, liveness, enrolment, privacy, is engineering around those four steps.**


The embedding idea comes from FaceNet, which trained a network so that the Euclidean distance between two face vectors directly measured how likely they were the same person [1]. ArcFace sharpened it with an angular margin loss that spreads identities further apart, and it is the recipe behind most open models today [2].

I built FaceVision in 2026 as a browser-only detection, recognition and liveness system: the camera frames never leave the device, only embeddings are sent to a FastAPI and PostgreSQL backend, and no image is ever stored [13]. This page is what that build taught me, with the papers underneath each step.

> The moment you decide never to store a face image, half your privacy problems disappear and the other half become simple. Store the vector, throw away the pixels.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour, from building FaceVision</cite>

## What is the difference between face detection and face recognition?

**Face detection finds faces: it returns bounding boxes and usually landmarks for eyes, nose and mouth, for every face in a frame, and it does not know or care who they are. Face recognition takes one detected face and identifies or verifies the person. Detection is the first stage of recognition, but a security camera that counts people, or a phone that focuses on a face, needs only detection.**



MTCNN was the standard detector for years [3]; RetinaFace improved accuracy on small and turned faces and remains a strong default [4]. Google's MediaPipe ships a fast detector that runs on phones and in browsers [11].

## What is a face embedding, and how are faces compared?

**A face embedding is a fixed-length vector, often 128 or 512 numbers, produced by a network trained so that the same person's faces cluster together and different people's faces sit apart. Comparison is a distance: cosine similarity or Euclidean distance between two vectors. If the distance is below a threshold, the system calls it a match. The threshold is not part of the model; it is a decision you make from your own error data.**



The embedding is why you never need to store the face image. A vector cannot be turned back into a photograph in any useful way, it is far smaller, and it can be compared in a database index like any other vector. FaceVision stores exactly this: the vector, the user id, the timestamp, nothing visual [13].

## How do I choose the match threshold?

**Collect pairs of embeddings from your real users and cameras, labelled same-person or different-person, then plot the two error rates as the threshold moves: false accepts, a stranger let in, and false rejects, the right person turned away. Choose the threshold that meets your risk. A door lock wants false accepts near zero and tolerates retries; a class attendance system tolerates a few false accepts and hates queues. Never ship a vendor's default threshold blind.**



NIST's ongoing Face Recognition Technology Evaluation publishes false match and false non-match rates for hundreds of algorithms under controlled conditions, and it is the reference for what state-of-the-art accuracy looks like [5]. It also shows how far the same algorithm's numbers move between a mugshot-quality image and a webcam frame, which is why your own data matters more than the leaderboard.

## Why does face recognition fail?

**For a short list of reasons that repeat everywhere: low light and backlight, motion blur, extreme pose, masks and sunglasses, low-resolution or heavily compressed cameras, faces too small in the frame, enrolment photos that look nothing like daily conditions, and a threshold tuned on a different population. Twins and close relatives are a real limit for some models. Most "the AI is broken" tickets are a camera or lighting problem.**



On twins: FaceVision, like every embedding system I have tested, sometimes cannot separate identical twins at a threshold that still rejects strangers. For high-stakes use, that is a reason to add a second factor, not a reason to loosen the threshold.

## Is face recognition biased, and how accurate is it across groups?

**Accuracy differs across demographic groups for most algorithms. NIST's 2019 demographic study measured higher false positive rates for some groups than others, with the size of the gap depending strongly on the algorithm [6]. The gap has narrowed in recent evaluations but has not vanished. The practical response is to test on your own user population, report the error rates per group, and choose a threshold and a fallback that protect the worst-served group, not the average.**


For a college attendance system in Kanpur, the relevant test set is your own students under your own classroom lights, not a benchmark shot in a studio elsewhere.

## What is liveness detection, and why do I need it?

**Liveness detection, also called presentation attack detection, checks that the face in front of the camera is a live person and not a printed photo, a phone screen showing a photo or video, or a mask. Without it, any recognition system that unlocks or pays can be defeated by a picture from social media. Active liveness asks the user to do something, blink, turn, follow a dot. Passive liveness analyses a single frame or short clip for texture, depth cues and screen artefacts.**



ISO/IEC 30107 defines the framework and terminology for presentation attack detection and the metrics vendors quote [7]. Texture analysis, the observation that a re-photographed face carries colour and frequency artefacts a live face does not, is one of the classic passive approaches [8]. FaceVision uses a passive check on the device before any embedding is computed, so a photo held to the camera is rejected before it can even be compared [13].


## Can I run face recognition in the browser, without a server seeing the face?

**Yes. ONNX Runtime Web runs detection, recognition and liveness models in the browser using WebAssembly or WebGPU [10]. The camera frame stays on the device, the models produce an embedding locally, and only the embedding travels to your API for comparison and storage. It is slower than a GPU server for large galleries, but for verification and small identification sets it is fast enough, and it removes the biggest privacy and compliance burden: you never possess a face image.**


The architecture of FaceVision, which is the concrete version of this answer:


Models are exported to ONNX from PyTorch or taken from open toolkits such as InsightFace, which publishes ArcFace-family recognition models and RetinaFace detectors [9]. Quantising them shrinks download size and speeds inference on phones, at a small accuracy cost you should measure.

## How do I build a face recognition attendance system?

**Enrol each person with three to five embeddings taken under the real classroom conditions, on the same kind of camera. At check-in, detect, run liveness, embed and compare against the enrolled set for that class only, which keeps the gallery small and the false-match rate low. Log the score, not the image. Add a fallback for rejections, such as a one-time code, so a bad lighting day does not stop a class. Publish the privacy notice before the first day.**


Attendance is the most common student project in this space and the one most often built wrong: images saved to a folder, a global gallery of thousands, no liveness, a threshold copied from a tutorial. Built right, with per-class galleries, on-device liveness and embeddings-only storage, it is also a strong portfolio piece, because you can explain each decision.

## Is face recognition legal in India, and how do I handle privacy?

**Facial data is biometric personal data, and India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, sets the framework for processing personal data with notice, consent, purpose limitation and security obligations [12]. Rules and enforcement continue to develop, so treat this as the direction, not legal advice. The engineering answer is independent of jurisdiction: collect consent, tell people what is stored and for how long, store embeddings rather than images, delete on request, and restrict who can run a search.**



I wrote a longer note on what changed in my own practice after FaceVision, and most of it is the list above [14].

## Which library or model should I use for face recognition?

**For a Python prototype: InsightFace for detection and ArcFace-family recognition, or the face_recognition library for simplicity at lower accuracy [9]. For phones and browsers: MediaPipe for detection [11] and an ONNX-exported ArcFace model in ONNX Runtime Web for recognition [10]. For anything that unlocks or pays: add a liveness model and test it against printed photos and phone screens yourself before you believe its numbers.**



## What are common face recognition interview questions?

**Explain detection versus recognition versus verification versus identification. Explain what an embedding is and why distance measures similarity. Explain how you would set a threshold and what false accept and false reject mean. Explain what liveness detection defends against. Explain how you would design the system so no face image is stored. If you can answer these from a project you built, you are ahead of most candidates.**



## Where should I start with a face recognition project?

**Build verification first, not identification: enrol yourself and two friends, run detection and embedding in the browser with ONNX Runtime Web, store only embeddings, and plot your own false accept and false reject curve from a hundred attempts. Then add passive liveness and try to fool it with a photo of yourself. That project teaches every concept on this page and is exactly the shape of FaceVision.**


If your college wants a hands-on session on computer vision that respects privacy from the first line of code, that is one of the talks I offer. Email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.
