# How to get an AI internship as a student in India: where to apply, the portfolio that gets replies, cold emails that work, and what to do when your college has no placements
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-get-an-ai-internship/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## How do I get an AI internship as a student?

**Build three live projects that look like the work, put them on a GitHub profile a recruiter can read in two minutes, and apply where AI work is visible: startups, agencies and small product companies, through their websites, founders' inboxes and the events they sponsor. Large companies mostly hire interns through campus programmes with degree and college filters; do not spend your energy fighting that filter in year two. My own first work came through a community I built and hackathons I entered, not through a placement cell, and that route is open to every student reading this.**


The longer versions of the outreach and the year-two decision are on the portfolio [8][9]. This is the operational page.

> Nobody replied to my resume. People replied to a link where they could click on something I had built and it worked.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## Which companies actually hire AI interns?

**Three kinds, in the order you should approach them. Startups and small product companies shipping AI features: they need hands, hire on portfolios, and a founder reads the inbox. Agencies and studios building AI for clients, such as the one I lead engineering for: varied projects, real deadlines, fast learning. Research labs and large companies: structured programmes, degree filters, campus channels, worth applying to but not worth waiting on. Remote-first companies abroad hire Indian students on portfolios and time-zone overlap.**



## Where should I look for AI internships?

**Internshala and Unstop for volume in India, filtered hard for roles that mention specific work, RAG, LLM, computer vision, not "AI intern" alone [1][4]. Wellfound for startups, including remote [2]. LinkedIn Jobs with alerts for your city plus the stack [3]. Google Summer of Code for paid open-source work with mentors [5]. Devfolio and other hackathon platforms, because sponsors recruit from the teams they watch [6]. And the inboxes of founders whose products you have used, which is where the best internships I know of came from.**


## What projects get internship replies?

**Three, each live at a URL with a README and a two-minute demo video. A RAG assistant over a real document set with measured retrieval recall. A small fine-tuned model with a base-versus-tuned comparison. One useful web app that a real person uses, even if that person is your club. Together they prove retrieval, training, evaluation and shipping. Match one of them to each company you write to; the reply rate on a matched project is many times that of a generic resume.**



The projects that get interviews, with reasons, are written up separately [10], and the GitHub profile that makes them findable is its own note [12].

## How do I write a cold email for an internship?

**Five sentences. Who you are and what you are studying, one line. One specific thing about their product or a recent post of theirs, which proves you looked. One link to a project of yours that resembles their work, with a one-line result. One specific ask: a four-to-eight-week internship on a named area, paid or unpaid stated plainly, remote or on-site. A thank-you. Under 120 words, from a real email address, with a subject line that names the company and the ask. Follow up once after a week.**


```
Subject: GenAI internship, RAG work, VSICS Kanpur student

Hi Neha,

I'm Aarav, second-year BCA at VSICS Kanpur. I used your document-search
product last month and noticed it returns whole pages rather than passages.

I built a RAG assistant over my college's syllabus with hybrid retrieval and
measured recall@10 of 0.9 on 40 real questions: <link to live demo and repo>.

Would you consider a six-week remote internship on retrieval quality this
summer? Paid or unpaid, I'd like to know which upfront.

Thank you for reading.
Aarav Singh · <portfolio> · +91 9xxxx xxxxx
```

Every line does a job. My longer notes on cold outreach, including what got replies and what did not, are on the portfolio [8].


## What if my college has no placement cell or AI companies do not visit?

**Then you are in my situation, and the route is the same one I took. Build the three projects. Start or join a community and teach in it, because communities are where referrals come from. Enter hackathons, in person when you can, because sponsors and judges hire. Contribute to an open-source project a target company uses. Post one build a week where engineers read. Apply remotely with the portfolio. The placement cell is one channel; these are five, and they work from any campus.**



## Should I take an unpaid internship, freelance instead, or start something?

**Take an unpaid internship only if the work is real, the mentor is real and it is short; otherwise freelance for small clients, which pays and teaches delivery, or build a product for a community you belong to. In year two I chose client work through the agency route and it taught more than any internship offer I had, but it is not the right answer for everyone. The decision framework is written up separately [9].**



## How do I get a remote AI internship?

**Portfolio first, writing second. Remote teams cannot see your college and do not care; they see your GitHub, your README and how clearly you write in email. Target companies that already hire remotely, contribute to their open-source tools, apply with a matching project, and be explicit about your time-zone overlap, which for Europe is India's structural advantage. Practise asynchronous communication by writing good READMEs and posts, because that is the interview.**


My notes on getting hired for remote AI work from India cover the companies and the communication habits in detail [11].

## How do I convert an internship into a job?

**Ship something visible in the first two weeks. Write a short weekly note of what you did and what you learned, and send it to your mentor. Take the unglamorous tasks and finish them completely. Ask questions in public channels so the team sees you learning. A month before the end, ask directly: what would it take to continue, and in what role? Most conversions happen because the intern asked, not because the company remembered.**




## What mistakes do students make applying for AI internships?

**Sending a resume with no links. Listing courses instead of projects. Applying only to large companies through portals. Generic emails to fifty founders. Projects that are tutorial clones with the name changed. A GitHub with one commit per project. Giving up after ten applications, when the pipeline needs a hundred. Waiting for the placement cell. Every one of these has a fix on this page.**



## Want help with your first application?

**I run career sessions for tech clubs that end with each student having a project pitch and a cold email drafted, and I review portfolios in mentoring sessions through TechVerse Enclave.** Email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# How to give a guest lecture in college: preparing a technical talk, handling Q&A, and becoming a speaker colleges invite back
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-give-a-guest-lecture-in-college/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## How do I get invited to give a guest lecture at a college?

**Do something specific, describe it in public, and make it easy to book you. Colleges and tech clubs invite people whose credential fits in one sentence, "shipped five production AI apps", "won Changethon at IIT Roorkee", and who have a page or a post that shows what a session with them looks like. Start with your own college and clubs you belong to, offer a concrete topic and two dates, say it is free for students, and post about the first session the same week. The second invitation comes from the first post.**


My first sessions were at VSICS Kanpur, my own college, to first-years and to the coding club: a career roadmap, a session on AI in the software lifecycle, a debate [1][2][3]. Each one produced a post with photos, each post produced the next invitation, and the pattern has not changed since. A page listing the talks I offer, with formats and logistics, is what organisers now book from [8].

> Nobody invites you to talk about AI. They invite you to talk about the thing you built, because you are the only person who can.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What should a guest lecture cover?

**One outcome. Decide what students should be able to do on Monday because of your session, then build backwards. For first-years: a roadmap and permission to start. For second- and third-years: one skill demonstrated live and a project to try. For final-years: what the industry actually hires for and how to show it. A talk that covers a whole topic teaches nothing; a talk that changes one action teaches something.**



The three-year roadmap I gave 100+ first-years at the VSICS induction was one outcome: know what year one, two and three are for, and start year one this week [1].

## How do I structure a 60- or 90-minute technical talk?

**Open with a two-minute story that has a failure in it. Show the map: three or four ideas, on one slide, that the session will cover. Do one live demo of something real, ten minutes at most. Give the roadmap: what to do next, in order. Then stop early and take questions for the rest of the slot. Students remember the story, the demo and one line from the roadmap. Slides are cue cards with one idea each; nobody reads paragraphs on a screen.**



My full outline for a 90-minute GenAI session, with the demo and the roadmap slides, is written up on the portfolio [6].

## How do I prepare a guest lecture?

**Ask the organiser five questions: who is in the room and how many, what year, what they already know, what the room has, and what they want students to leave with. Write the one outcome. Build the demo first and rehearse it on the machine you will use. Then write slides, no more than one per two minutes. Rehearse once with a timer, once without slides, and cut a third. Arrive early and test the projector with your laptop.**



The longer version of how I prepare is on the portfolio [4]; the short version is that the demo is built before a single slide exists.

## How do I handle a quiet room or a difficult question?

**A quiet room is a setup problem. Ask a question with no wrong answer, "who here has used ChatGPT for an assignment?", raise your own hand, and wait a full five seconds. Take the first answer seriously and build on it. For a question you cannot answer, say so, say what you would check and how, and offer to follow up by email. For a hostile question, restate it calmly, answer the part that is fair, and move on. Students forgive not knowing; they do not forgive bluffing.**


I wrote a separate piece on handling Q&A after technical talks, because it is where most speakers either win or lose the room [5]. The single most useful habit: repeat every question aloud before answering, so the back row hears it and you get three seconds to think.


## Should I use slides, a demo or a whiteboard?

**All three, in that priority reversed: demo first, whiteboard for the one idea that needs drawing, slides as cue cards. A live demo of a real system is the part students talk about afterwards and the part that proves you have built things. A whiteboard sketch of an architecture lands harder than a diagram slide because they watch it appear. Slides carry structure, links and the roadmap. Never read from them.**



## Are guest lecturers paid? Should I charge?

**Some are, many are not, and universities often have fixed honoraria under their rules. I speak at student communities for free, on-site with travel covered or remote at no cost, because those rooms are where the people I want in the industry sit, and because I was helped the same way. Early on, speak for free and for the post. Later, charge companies and conferences, and keep colleges free if you can. Say your terms in your first reply so nobody is embarrassed.**


## How do I become a hackathon judge or mentor as well?

**The same way, one step further: attend hackathons, then mentor at one, then ask the organiser to sit on the panel. Organisers want judges who have built and shipped, who can brief a rubric and who show up on time. Once you have judged once, the invitations come with the speaking ones. Publish your rubric, because organisers copy it and remember where it came from.**


My path from participant to judge, and what organisers told me they look for, is written up separately [7].

## What mistakes do first-time speakers make?

**Covering everything. Reading slides. Forty minutes of context before anything concrete. A demo that has never run on the presenting laptop. No questions asked of the room until the end. Running over time into the next session. Bluffing an answer. Leaving without sharing slides or a way to reach you. Each is fixable before the session with the checklist above; none is fixable during it.**



## How do I turn one talk into a lasting relationship with a college?

**Send the slides and links within a day. Reply to every student email for a month. Post the photos and tag the college and the club. Then propose the next thing: a hands-on workshop, a judging slot at their hackathon, monthly office hours for the club. Three of my longest mentoring relationships with student clubs started as a single session followed by one email I bothered to send.**



## Where can I start speaking?

**At your own college's club, next month, on the thing you built last semester. Offer two dates, one topic and a demo. If you would like to see how I structure sessions, the talk menu and the 90-minute outline are public [6][8].** If your college wants a session, or wants a speaker to show your students how to become speakers, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# How to improve your public speaking for tech talks: structure, nerves, filler words, and the practice that actually moves the needle
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-improve-public-speaking-for-tech-talks/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## How do I actually get better at public speaking for tech talks?

**By practising the specific talk out loud, repeatedly, more than by practising "public speaking" as a general skill. Generic advice, power poses, deep breathing, helps a little with nerves in the moment, but the bigger lever for a technical talk is structure: a clear problem, a logical build, a strong close, rehearsed enough times that you are not simultaneously thinking about content and delivery. Most improvement comes from removing the specific things you are afraid of, forgetting what comes next, losing the room, running over time, one rehearsal at a time.**


I have given technical talks to rooms from twenty to several hundred students, and the improvement that actually showed up in feedback came almost entirely from rehearsal discipline, not from any general public-speaking technique.

> Confidence on stage is not a personality trait. It is the residue of having rehearsed the specific talk enough times that nothing in it can surprise you.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## Why does structure matter more than delivery style for a technical talk?

**Because an audience that cannot follow the logical thread of a talk will not be won over by good delivery, and an audience that can follow a clear structure will forgive an imperfect delivery. A technical talk needs a stated problem, a build toward the solution with one idea per section, and a close that restates what changed for the listener. Delivery, pace, tone, eye contact, matters, but it amplifies a structure that already works; it cannot rescue a talk that has no clear thread [3][4].**



## How do I handle nerves before and during a talk?

**Nerves rarely disappear with experience; they get quieter because thorough preparation removes the specific fears driving them. Rehearse the opening thirty seconds until it is close to memorised, since a strong start calms the rest of the talk. Arrive early enough to test the room's tech, slides, mic, clicker, so equipment surprises do not add to the nerves. Accept a slightly faster heartbeat as normal rather than fighting it, and use the first minute's adrenaline for energy rather than trying to suppress it entirely.**




## How do I cut filler words like "um" and "so"?

**Replace the filler with a deliberate silent pause instead of trying to suppress it through willpower alone; a pause reads as confidence, while "um" reads as searching. Filler words cluster at points where you have not fully decided what comes next, so the real fix is often tightening your structure and rehearsal, not a speech habit in isolation. Recording yourself and counting fillers in a five-minute segment makes the habit visible, which is usually enough to start correcting it, since most people underestimate how often they do it until they hear it back.**



## What is the single most effective practice habit?

**Rehearsing the actual talk out loud, standing, at full volume, as many times as the stakes justify, rather than silently reading slides or rehearsing only in your head. Silent rehearsal does not train the muscle memory of speaking, the timing, or where you actually stumble; those only show up when you say the words aloud. Recording one full out-loud rehearsal and watching it back, however uncomfortable, surfaces more fixable problems in ten minutes than a week of silent preparation.**



## How do I read a room and adjust in real time?

**Watch for the visible signals: heads down on phones, note-taking, confused frowns, nodding along, and adjust pace or depth accordingly, slowing down and adding an example when you see confusion, moving faster when you see impatience. This is trainable by deliberately watching the room instead of only your slides or notes during rehearsal-adjacent early talks, and by asking a trusted person in the audience to flag specific moments afterward where the room's energy visibly shifted.**


## What mistakes do people make trying to improve their public speaking?

**Practising general public-speaking exercises instead of the actual talk they need to give. Reading slides silently and calling it rehearsal. Trying to eliminate nerves entirely instead of channelling them. Adding more content when a talk runs long instead of cutting it, which makes nerves worse under time pressure. Never recording themselves, so the gap between how a talk feels and how it actually sounds stays invisible.**



## Public speaking interview and evaluation questions

**"Tell me about a time you presented to a group" is asked in almost every interview, technical or not, and the strongest answers describe a specific talk, its structure, and what you changed after getting feedback, not a general claim of being "good at public speaking". Toastmasters-style structured feedback, or simply asking a trusted listener for one specific thing to improve, builds this evidence faster than unstructured practice alone [1].**



## Where should I start?

**Record yourself giving your next talk's opening two minutes, out loud, standing, and watch it back once. That single exercise usually surfaces more than a week of reading advice.** For a workshop on technical public speaking for students and early-career engineers, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# How to invite a guest speaker to your college: the email, the one-pager, fees, logistics and what makes a speaker say yes
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-invite-a-guest-speaker-to-your-college/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## How do I invite a guest speaker to my college?

**Send one clear email with six things: who you are and which club or department you represent, who will be in the room and how many, two or three proposed dates with a time window, the format and duration you want, the topic you hope they will cover and the outcome you want for students, and what you can offer, travel, a certificate, a recording, a meal. Then follow up once after five days. Speakers say yes to invitations that make the decision easy.**


I receive these invitations regularly, and the ones I accept fastest share a shape. This is the template, written from the receiving end, with what actually decides a yes [1].

> "Can you come and speak about AI?" is the most common invitation I get and the hardest to say yes to, because "AI" is not a talk. "Can you run a 90-minute session on building a RAG system for 60 third-years on 12 or 19 October?" is a talk.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What should the invitation email say?

**Subject: "Guest session on [topic] for [college], [month]". Body: one line on who you are, one on the audience, the two dates, the format, the topic and outcome, the offer, and a link to your club's page or last event. Under 200 words. Attach nothing; link instead. Sign with a name, a role and a phone number.**


```
Subject: Guest session on GenAI engineering for VSICS Kanpur, October

Hi Pranjul,

I'm Aditi, secretary of the coding club at VSICS Kanpur. We run monthly
sessions for 60 to 80 second- and third-year BCA and B.Tech students.

Would you run a 90-minute session on building a RAG system, ending with
students having a working demo? Proposed dates: Sat 12 Oct or Sat 19 Oct,
11:00 to 12:30, in our seminar hall (projector, Wi-Fi, 80 seats).

We can cover travel within Kanpur, provide a certificate and lunch, and
will post photos and a recap tagging you the same week.

Last month's session: <link>. Happy to adjust the topic to your menu.

Aditi Sharma, Coding Club, VSICS Kanpur, +91 98xxx xxxxx
```

Every sentence answers a question the speaker would otherwise have to ask. That is the whole trick.

## How do I find a guest speaker for a college event?

**Start with alumni working in the field, then practitioners in your city, then people who already post about speaking at colleges on LinkedIn. Search LinkedIn for your city plus the topic and "workshop" or "session", check who has spoken at nearby colleges' events, ask community organisers at Google Developer Groups on Campus or Microsoft Learn Student Ambassadors chapters, and look at who judges local hackathons. People who already give their time to students are the ones who will give it to you.**



Community programmes such as Google Developer Groups on Campus and Microsoft Learn Student Ambassadors exist partly to connect chapters with speakers, and their organisers know who is active in your region [6][7]. Major League Hacking's community does the same for hackathon-adjacent speakers [8].

## Are guest speakers paid? What does a guest lecturer cost?

**It varies. Many working engineers, including me, speak at student communities for free, on-site with travel covered or remote at no cost, because that is how we were helped. Professional speakers and senior executives often charge a fee. Universities sometimes have a fixed honorarium for guest lecturers under their academic rules. Ask directly in the first email: "We can offer travel and a certificate; if you have a fee, please tell us." Nobody is offended by that sentence.**


My own rule: free for student communities and colleges, on-site anywhere in India with travel covered, remote anywhere at no cost [3]. The reason is not generosity; it is that the students in those rooms are exactly the people I want in the community and, later, in the industry.

## What topics should I ask a speaker to cover?

**Ask for a topic that ends with students able to do something, not knowing something. "Build a RAG system in 90 minutes", "How hackathon judges score, from a judge", "From BCA to GenAI engineer: the roadmap", "Ship your first AI app for free". Pick from the speaker's own menu if they publish one, and say which of your students it is for: first-years need a roadmap; final-years need a project and interview preparation.**



The five talks I offer, with the audience each is built for, are listed on the portfolio [2]. Most practitioners who speak regularly have a similar page; asking for one of their listed talks gets a faster yes than asking them to invent one.

## What does a speaker need from the organisers?

**A one-pager a week before the event: the exact venue and how to reach it, the audience size and year, start and end times, the schedule around their slot, the tech setup, projector input, Wi-Fi, microphone, whiteboard, two contact numbers, and what you will need from them, a bio, a photo, a title. On the day: someone to meet them, water, a working projector tested with their laptop, and a hard stop you protect.**



The single most common failure I see is the projector: a laptop that will not connect, an adapter nobody has, ten minutes of the session gone. Test with the speaker's actual laptop, or ask them to send slides to run from yours.


## How do I introduce a guest speaker?

**In under a minute: their name, what they do now, one specific thing they have built or achieved that this audience will respect, why they are here today, and their name again. Do not read their whole LinkedIn. Do not list every award. One concrete credential lands harder than ten adjectives.**


For example: "Pranjul Rathour is a GenAI engineer from Kanpur who shipped five production AI systems this year and won first prize at Changethon at IIT Roorkee. He did his BCA at this college. He's here to show you how a RAG system is actually built. Please welcome Pranjul." Forty seconds, done.

## What is the difference between a guest lecture, a seminar, a workshop and a webinar?

**A guest lecture is one expert speaking to a class, usually 45 to 90 minutes with questions. A seminar is a session built around discussion, often with several speakers or student presentations. A workshop is hands-on: students build or practise something with the speaker's guidance, and it needs laptops, more time and a smaller room. A webinar is any of these delivered online. Ask for the format that matches your goal: a lecture to inspire, a workshop to equip.**



## How do I get a speaker for a remote or online session?

**The same email, minus travel, plus the platform you will use and whether you will record. Remote sessions are the easiest yes a speaker can give, so use them for speakers outside your city, for shorter formats and for follow-ups after an in-person session. Test the platform with the speaker for five minutes the day before, assign a moderator to read questions, and send the recording link within a week.**


I speak remotely for any student community anywhere at no cost, which is true of many practitioners; the constraint is never the speaker's willingness, it is whether the invitation is concrete [3].

## How do I turn one session into a lasting relationship?

**Post the photos and a recap the same week, tagging the speaker and the college. Send a two-line thank-you with one thing students did as a result. Then ask for the next specific thing: judging your hackathon, a follow-up workshop, an office-hours call for the club, feedback on three student projects. Speakers remember organisers who follow through, and the second yes is always faster than the first.**


Three of my longest mentoring relationships with student clubs started as one session; what they had in common was an organiser who wrote back a week later with photos and a question.


## What mistakes do organisers make?

**Vague topics. One date offered with no alternative. Asking two days before the event. No mention of the audience. Attachments instead of links. Forgetting to say whether the session is online or on-site. Not testing the projector. Ending late and eating into the speaker's next commitment. Never posting afterwards. Each is fixed by the checklist above, and each one I have experienced as a speaker.**



## Can I invite you?

**Yes. Send the six things above to pranjulrathour41@gmail.com, or use the invite page, which lists the five talks, the formats and the logistics I need [4].** Free for student communities, on-site across India with travel covered, remote anywhere. The abstract and bio come back the same day.

# How to learn Python for AI in 2026: the roadmap from zero to shipping an LLM app, what to skip, and the projects that prove it
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-learn-python-for-ai/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## How do I learn Python for AI?

**Learn the Python that ships software, then point it at models. In practice: variables, functions and data structures; reading and writing files and JSON; calling HTTP APIs; virtual environments and packages; classes when you need them; async when you have many calls; tests. Then, with that base, call a model API, build a small FastAPI service around it, and deploy it. Twelve weeks of building gets a beginner to a live LLM application. Twelve weeks of tutorials gets a beginner to week thirteen of tutorials.**


All five production AI systems I shipped in 2026 are Python services: a RAG platform, a fine-tuning platform, a document extraction service, a face recognition backend and an OCR and speech workspace [14]. The Python inside them is not exotic. It is the Python in this roadmap, used carefully, with tests.

> Nobody has ever asked me to reverse a linked list in Python at work. Everybody has asked me why the API call timed out. Learn for the second question.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## How much Python do I need for AI?

**Less than the tutorials suggest, and different. You need: core syntax and data structures; functions with type hints; modules and packages; file and JSON handling; error handling; HTTP requests; virtual environments; the standard library's pathlib, json, datetime, logging and asyncio; classes and dataclasses; and writing tests. You do not need, at first: metaclasses, decorators beyond using them, deep NumPy, or competitive-programming tricks. Those come when a project demands them.**



## What is the roadmap from zero to an AI app?

**Twelve weeks, four projects, each deployed. Weeks one to three: fundamentals through a command-line tool that reads a file and produces a report. Weeks four to six: HTTP and APIs through a script that calls a model API and saves structured output. Weeks seven to nine: a FastAPI service with a database, deployed on a free tier. Weeks ten to twelve: a RAG application over documents you know, with an evaluation set. Every week, one commit a day, and a README that explains what you built.**



The longer version, with resources per week, is on the portfolio [13].

## Which Python libraries matter for AI in 2026?

**For calling models: the provider SDKs, or plain httpx and requests [5][6]. For services: FastAPI with Pydantic for validation [4][7]. For data handling: json and pathlib from the standard library, pandas when tables appear. For retrieval: an embeddings client and pgvector or FAISS. For training and fine-tuning: PyTorch, Transformers, PEFT and TRL, learned when you fine-tune, not before. For tests: pytest [8]. For environments: uv or venv with pip [9]. Learn each when a project needs it.**



Frameworks such as LangChain are fine for a first prototype; I recommend calling the SDKs directly for your first real project so you understand every line you ship.

## Should I learn NumPy, pandas and maths first?

**No, not first. For an applications career in GenAI, you can build and deploy your first LLM app without NumPy. Learn pandas when you have a table to analyse, NumPy when you touch vectors directly, and the maths, linear algebra and probability, alongside your first embedding and fine-tuning projects, where it has a purpose. Learning them first is how students spend six months on prerequisites and never ship. For a research or classical ML path, reverse the order.**



## What are the best free resources to learn Python for AI?

**The official Python tutorial for the language itself [1]. Automate the Boring Stuff for practical scripting [2]. Python for Everybody for a gentle structured course [3]. FastAPI's documentation, which is a course in itself [4]. Hugging Face's free LLM course once you are calling models [10]. fast.ai for deep learning intuition when you get there [11]. Google Colab for a free notebook and GPU [12]. All free. Pick one per stage, finish it by building, and do not collect courses.**



## What should my first Python AI project be?

**A script that reads a folder of your own notes or PDFs, calls a model API to summarise each one into structured JSON, validates the JSON with Pydantic, and writes a report. It touches files, HTTP, error handling, structured data and tests, and it is useful to you. Then wrap it in FastAPI and deploy it. Then add retrieval so you can ask questions across the notes. Three steps, three months, one growing project, live at a URL.**


```python
import json
from pathlib import Path
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Summary(BaseModel):
    title: str
    key_points: list[str]
    open_questions: list[str]

def summarise(path: Path) -> Summary:
    text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    raw = call_model(f"Summarise into JSON with title, key_points, open_questions:\n\n{text}")
    return Summary.model_validate_json(raw)          # fails loudly if the model drifts

report = [summarise(p).model_dump() for p in Path("notes").glob("*.md")]
Path("report.json").write_text(json.dumps(report, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
```

That is a week-four project, and a version of it is the seed of every document system I have shipped.

## What mistakes keep students stuck in Python tutorials?

**Watching instead of typing. Starting a fourth course before deploying a first project. Learning NumPy for months before calling a single API. Skipping virtual environments and losing a week to dependency conflicts. Never writing a test, so every change is scary. Copying assistant output without reading it. Treating tracebacks as failures instead of instructions. The fix for all of them is the same: ship something small every week and read the errors.**


## Python for AI interview questions

**Expect practical Python: parse and validate JSON, write a retry with backoff around an API call, chunk text by paragraphs with a size cap, compute cosine similarity, use a dict to count or group, write a small async fan-out over many API calls, and write a test for one of those. Rarely puzzles. Interviewers want typed, readable code and a candidate who talks through edge cases; the coding round for GenAI roles is a work sample, not an exam.**





## Where should I start today?

**Install Python, create a virtual environment, and write a script that reads one file and prints a summary of it. Tomorrow make the summary come from a model API. By the weekend, put it in a repository with a README.** For a workshop at your college that takes a room from zero Python to a deployed AI app, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# How to negotiate your first tech job offer in India: what freshers can actually negotiate, the script, and the mistakes that cost the most
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-negotiate-your-first-tech-job-offer/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## Can a fresher actually negotiate a tech job offer?

**Yes, more often than freshers assume, and the ask itself carries almost no risk when done politely and after the offer is already extended. Companies build a negotiation buffer into most offers precisely because they expect some candidates to ask; a fresher who never asks simply leaves that buffer on the table. The risk people fear, the offer being pulled for asking, is genuinely rare for a reasonable, polite ask after an offer letter exists; it happens far more often as a scare story than as a real outcome.**


Most students I mentor accept the first number out of fear the offer will vanish if they ask for anything; watching that fear turn out to be misplaced, again and again, is why this page exists.

> The worst realistic outcome of a polite, reasonable ask is "no, this is final." The worst outcome of never asking is guaranteed: you get exactly the first number, every time.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What is actually negotiable in an entry-level offer?

**The base salary is the most visible lever, but rarely the only one. Joining bonus, sometimes easier to move than base since it is a one-time cost to the company. Start date, useful if you need time to finish exams, travel, or simply breathe between college and work. Remote or hybrid flexibility, where the role allows it. Sign-on equipment or relocation support. Even the level or designation, in some structures, if your background genuinely supports it. Ask about the whole package, not only the headline number, since some of these move more easily than base pay does.**



## How do I know what to ask for?

**Research real compensation data for the specific company, role and level before naming a number, using sources like Levels.fyi and Glassdoor rather than guessing [1][2]. Anchor your ask to that data, not to a vague sense that "more would be nice." A specific, researched ask, "I've seen this role bands around X for this level, is there room to move closer to that," is far more persuasive than an unspecific "can you do better."**



## What is the actual script for negotiating without a competing offer?

**Thank them for the offer, confirm genuine enthusiasm for the role, then ask specifically and briefly: "I'm excited about this role. Based on what I've seen for similar positions at this level, is there flexibility on the base salary?" No bluff, no ultimatum, no apology. If the answer is no on base, ask about the joining bonus or start date next, since a single "no" on one lever does not mean no on all of them.**



## Do I need a competing offer to negotiate?

**It helps, because it gives the company a concrete number to react to, but it is not required. A well-researched, specific, polite ask moves numbers on its own more often than people expect, especially for a first offer where companies have built in some room precisely because they expect this conversation. Never bluff about a competing offer you do not have; it is easily discoverable through informal networks, and being caught bluffing costs far more trust than simply not having leverage in the first place.**



## What mistakes cost the most in salary negotiation?

**Bluffing about an offer that does not exist, which is discoverable and destroys trust immediately if caught. Negotiating over email in a way that reads as an ultimatum instead of a conversation. Accepting a verbal promise of a later raise instead of getting the actual number in the offer letter. Negotiating only the base and never asking about the rest of the package. Being so afraid of losing the offer that the ask never happens at all, guaranteeing the outcome you were afraid of by default.**



## Salary negotiation interview and follow-up questions

**Recruiters sometimes ask directly what compensation you are expecting; answer with a researched range, not a vague deflection or an unresearched high number. If pressed for your current or previous salary where legally relevant, answer honestly but redirect to the value you bring for this specific role rather than anchoring entirely to a past number.**



## Where should I start?

**Before you accept your next offer, look up real compensation data for that company and role, and ask one specific, polite question about the number. That single habit, repeated at every offer for the rest of your career, compounds.** For a career session on negotiating your first tech offer, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# How to participate in your first hackathon: where to find hackathons in India, how to form a team, what to prepare, and what to expect in 24 to 48 hours
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-participate-in-your-first-hackathon/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## How do I participate in a hackathon for the first time?

**Find one on Devfolio, Unstop, MLH, Devpost or Hack2skill that welcomes beginners, register two to four weeks ahead, form a team of two to four through the event's team-finding channel or your college, set up your laptop and accounts the week before, and arrive with one small idea you could finish in half the time available. Then build the smallest working version, demo it honestly, and write down what you learned. The first hackathon teaches you how hackathons work; the second one is where you start winning.**


My first hackathon was a mess: a team that met at registration, an idea that needed three days, a demo that did not run. Three later wins came from doing the opposite of everything on that day [8]. This page is what I wish someone had handed me before the first one.

> Nobody wins their first hackathon by being brilliant. They win their fourth by having learned what the first three taught.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What is a hackathon, and what actually happens?

**A hackathon is a timed building competition, usually 24 to 48 hours, where small teams build a working prototype around a theme or a problem statement and demo it to judges. It opens with a briefing and problem statements, then the build, with mentors circulating and checkpoints or mid-way reviews, then submissions with a repository and a video, then three-minute pitches, then results. Online hackathons run the same way over Discord and a submission portal. Food, sleep and the demo working are the three things beginners underestimate.**



## Where do I find hackathons in India?

**Devfolio lists most large student hackathons in India, including college fests, and has team-finding built in [1]. Unstop lists corporate and college hackathons plus case competitions [2]. Major League Hacking runs a global season of student hackathons with many in India [3]. Devpost is where company-sponsored online hackathons live [4]. Hack2skill hosts corporate and government-partnered events [5]. Smart India Hackathon is the national one, run through your college [6]. Beyond the platforms, follow your college's coding club, nearby college fests, and community Discord and WhatsApp groups, where smaller, beginner-friendly events appear first.**



## How do I get shortlisted?

**Most hackathons with more applicants than seats shortlist on the application. Fill in every field. Link a GitHub with at least two repositories that have READMEs, even small ones. Write the "why do you want to attend" answer specifically: what you want to build or learn, not "to gain experience". If the hackathon asks for an idea, give a small concrete one. Apply early; late applications compete for fewer seats. Apply to several; acceptance is partly luck.**


## How do I find a hackathon team?

**Post in the event's team-finding channel, on Devfolio or Discord, with three lines: what you can do, what you want to learn, and when you are free to talk. Ask in your college coding club and your class group. Say yes to a team that has a skill you lack, even if you do not know them. A team of three with one person who can build a frontend, one who can build a backend or model, and one who can design and pitch is enough. Two committed people beat four who vanish at midnight.**



The longer version of finding a team, including how to handle a teammate who disappears mid-event, is on the portfolio [9].


## What should I prepare the week before?

**The boring things that eat hours on the day. Laptop updated, editor and Python or Node set up, Git configured, GitHub account with SSH working. Accounts created and API keys tested for the tools you might use, kept in a `.env` file. A starter template you have run once: a frontend, an API, a database, deployed somewhere free. A charger, an extension cord, a power bank, headphones, a water bottle, snacks, a change of clothes for offline events. And a plan for the demo video, because recording at 6 a.m. with no plan is how good projects submit bad videos.**



## What should a beginner build at a hackathon?

**One feature that works end to end, for one specific person, with a demo you can show in ninety seconds. A receipt reader for a hostel mess. A notice-board summariser for your college WhatsApp. A form that fills itself from a photo. Use APIs for the hard parts and spend your hours on the flow and the demo. Do not build a platform, a marketplace, a social network or anything with "ecosystem" in the description. The judging rewards a thing that runs, and beginners lose by attempting things that cannot run in 36 hours.**



My list of what to build at a first hackathon, with the scope test I still use, is written up separately [10].

## How do I manage the 24 to 48 hours?

**Decide the idea and the demo path in the first hour and do not revisit it. Split work by interface: one person owns the frontend, one the backend, one the model or data, with the API contract written down first. Have something that runs end to end, however ugly, by the halfway mark. Eat on a schedule. Sleep in shifts if it is overnight; a team with two hours of sleep each builds better than a team with none. Freeze the build with two hours left. Record the video and rehearse the pitch on the frozen build.**



## What if I do not know how to code well yet?

**Come anyway, with a role. Teams need someone to design screens, write the pitch, make the video, test the flow, talk to mentors and keep the plan. Learn one thing during the event by pairing with the builder on one small piece. Use no-code and low-code tools for parts of the demo where they fit. Judges care whether the thing works and whether the team understood the problem, not whether every member wrote code. By your second hackathon you will have shipped something, which is the fastest way to learn to code well.**


## How do I make the first hackathon count even if I lose?

**Ship something that runs, however small. Talk to at least three mentors and two other teams. Write down what broke and why. Post about it the same week with a screenshot, the lesson and a thank-you to the organisers. Keep the repository clean with a README and a video link. Add the event to your LinkedIn as experience. Register for the next one before the memory fades. Every win I have had traces back to a loss I wrote about.**



## Hackathon FAQ for beginners

**Do I need a team? Most events allow solo, but a team of two or three is easier and more fun. Do I need an idea before? Usually not; problem statements come at the start, and platforms often let you form teams first. Is it free? Student hackathons almost always are, and offline ones usually feed you. Can first-years join? Yes, and many events have first-timer tracks. Online or offline? Offline for the first one if you can; the energy and the mentors help.**



## Where should I start?

**Open Devfolio or Unstop tonight, pick one hackathon four weeks out, register, and post a three-line team-finding message. The rest of this page applies from there.** For a hackathon workshop at your college that covers picking, building and pitching in a weekend, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# How to prepare a dataset for fine-tuning an LLM: formats, chat templates, how much data, synthetic data, validation and the checklist before you train
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-prepare-a-dataset-for-fine-tuning/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## How do I prepare a dataset for fine-tuning an LLM?

**Start with a written spec of the behaviour you want, then collect or write examples that follow it exactly: for each, the input a user would give and the ideal output, in the chat format the base model expects. Deduplicate, validate every row against the spec, hold out a validation split, measure token lengths, and read a random sample by eye. The dataset is the fine-tune; the training run only copies what is in it, including its inconsistencies.**


FineTune Studio, the platform I built in 2026, validates the uploaded dataset before it lets a run start, because the most common reason a run produced a bad model had nothing to do with hyper-parameters: the data was inconsistent, mis-templated or leaked into the validation split [12]. This page is that validation, explained.

> Write twenty examples by hand before anything else. If twenty consistent examples are hard to write, the spec is not ready, and the fine-tune will faithfully learn the confusion.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour, from building FineTune Studio</cite>

## What should the spec contain?

**One paragraph: who the user is, what they send, what the model must produce, in what format, with what tone, and what it must do when the input is unclear or out of scope. Then three example pairs that follow it. Every later example is checked against this paragraph. A spec you cannot write in a paragraph is a task you are not ready to train.**


## Which dataset format should I use: Alpaca, ShareGPT or chat messages?

**Use the messages format, a list of role and content turns, system, user, assistant, because it maps directly onto the chat template every modern model uses and onto what TRL's trainer expects [7]. Alpaca's instruction, input and output fields [1] and ShareGPT's multi-turn conversations are older JSON shapes that convert to messages trivially. The format is a container; what the model actually sees is the template rendered from it.**



A row in the messages format, which is also the shape most APIs accept [9]:

```json
{"messages": [
  {"role": "system", "content": "You are a support agent for Acme. Answer only from the provided policy. If the policy does not cover the question, say so and offer to escalate."},
  {"role": "user", "content": "Policy: Refunds within 14 days with receipt.\n\nQuestion: I bought it 20 days ago, can I return it?"},
  {"role": "assistant", "content": "The policy allows refunds within 14 days of purchase with a receipt, so a return at 20 days is outside the window. I can escalate this to a supervisor if you would like."}
]}
```

## What is a chat template and why does it matter?

**A chat template is the exact string layout a model was trained on for conversations: the special tokens that mark the start and end of each turn and which role speaks. Every model family uses a different one. If you train with the wrong template, or hand-write the tokens with a small mistake, the model learns garbage or produces it at inference. Always render examples with the tokenizer's own template function [6], and use the same template when you serve the model.**


```python
from transformers import AutoTokenizer
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(BASE)
text = tok.apply_chat_template(row["messages"], tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=False)
# never build this string by hand; the template lives with the model
```

Template mismatch is the single most common cause of a fine-tuned chat model that "does not work", in my experience and in the support questions FineTune Studio users asked. My longer note on formats and templates is on the portfolio [11].

## How much data do I need to fine-tune an LLM?

**For tone, style and output format: a few hundred high-quality examples produce a visible, stable change. For a classification or extraction skill: a few thousand covering the classes and the edge cases. For adapting to a domain's language: tens of thousands. Below about a hundred, put the examples in the prompt instead. LIMA showed that a thousand carefully curated examples were enough to teach strong instruction-following, and that quality mattered more than quantity [2].**



These are orders of magnitude from experience, not laws; the only reliable number comes from training on half your data and checking whether the other half still improves the model.

## Can I use synthetic data for fine-tuning?

**Yes, and most fine-tuning datasets today are partly synthetic: a stronger model generates examples from your spec, from seed examples, or from documents. Self-Instruct and Alpaca showed the approach at scale [3][1]. It works when you filter hard: validate every generated row against the spec, remove duplicates and near-duplicates, spot-check by hand, and mix in real examples so the model does not learn the generator's tics and refusals. Unfiltered synthetic data teaches a copy of the generator, not your task.**



## How do I clean and deduplicate the dataset?

**Normalise whitespace and encoding. Remove exact duplicates, then near-duplicates by comparing normalised text or embeddings, because duplicated training data both wastes compute and makes models memorise [5]. Remove rows that violate the spec: wrong format, wrong language, refusals you did not intend, outputs that reference the prompt. Strip personal data you do not have consent to train on. Measure token lengths and trim or split outliers so no row exceeds your training sequence length.**



The Hugging Face Datasets library handles the mechanics, loading, mapping, filtering and splitting, for datasets of any size [8]. My own pre-training validation checklist, which FineTune Studio runs automatically, is written up separately [10].


## How do I split training and validation data?

**Hold out ten to twenty percent, chosen so that near-duplicates of a training row never land in validation, or the validation loss lies to you. For grouped data, all rows from one document, one user or one conversation go to the same split. Keep a third, small test set of examples you wrote by hand and never look at during tuning, for the final honest comparison of base versus fine-tuned.**


## What is label masking, and should I train on the user turns?

**Label masking means computing the loss only on the assistant's tokens, so the model learns to produce answers rather than to predict the user's questions. Most trainers do this for you when you use the messages format with a chat template and an assistant-only loss option [7]. Training on user turns wastes capacity and can teach the model to continue user text. Mask them unless you have a specific reason not to.**


## What are common dataset mistakes?

**Mixing two specs in one dataset, so the model learns to flip between them. Hand-writing chat tokens. Duplicated rows inflating confidence. A validation split that shares documents with training. Outputs that mention the instruction. Ten variations of the same easy example and none of the hard cases. Personal data nobody consented to. Not reading any rows. A model can only be as consistent as its data, and it will be exactly as inconsistent.**



## Dataset interview questions

**How much data do you need for a style fine-tune versus a skill? What is a chat template and what happens if you get it wrong? How do you generate synthetic data without teaching the generator's habits? How do you prevent leakage between splits? What is label masking? Each answer above is a paragraph; the best evidence is a dataset you built and a model whose behaviour you can trace to specific rows.**



## Where should I start?

**Pick one narrow behaviour, write the paragraph spec and twenty examples tonight, render them with the tokenizer's template, and read them back. Then generate two hundred more synthetically, filter them against the spec, and hold out twenty. That dataset will fine-tune a small model on a free GPU tomorrow.** For a hands-on fine-tuning workshop at your college, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# How to start a tech community on campus: from five friends to 500 members, the sessions, the structure and the mistakes, from building TechVerse Enclave
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-start-a-tech-community-on-campus/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## How do I start a tech community on campus?

**Pick one topic you can teach for an hour, book a room, tell five people, and run the session this week. Then run one next week. A community is a weekly session that happens whether five or fifty people attend; everything else, the name, the logo, the group chat, the sponsors, comes after the habit exists. TechVerse Enclave started in 2023 as a hackathon team and a handful of friends learning web development together. It has since grown past 500 members, and I have mentored more than 200 students through it. The first six months were the hardest and the most important.**


The full playbook, with the timeline and the numbers, is on the portfolio [1][3]. This page is the version for someone starting Monday.

> Nobody joins a community. They come to a session, and they come back to the next one because it happened. The community is the coming back.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour, founder of TechVerse Enclave</cite>

## What should the first session be?

**Something you built last month, shown live, then a hands-on hour where everyone leaves with a version running. A first session about "introduction to AI" attracts fifty curious people who never return. A first session where ten people deploy their first web page attracts ten people who return with friends. Teach what you know; the second session can be taught by whoever learned fastest.**



The session format I still use, with timings, is written up separately [4]: ten minutes of story, twenty of demonstration, forty of hands-on, and a public artefact from every attendee.

## How do I get people to show up and keep coming?

**Same time, same place, every week, announced the day before, with photos and a recap the same day. Make the first-timer's experience good: someone greets them, the setup instructions were sent in advance, they leave with something working. Ask every attendee to bring one person. Celebrate small ships publicly. Growth came for TechVerse Enclave when members started teaching, because each new teacher brought their own circle.**



## How should a student community be organised?

**Small roles with names: a lead, a sessions lead who owns the calendar, a content lead who posts, an outreach lead who invites speakers and talks to faculty, and a treasurer if money exists. A shared calendar planned a month ahead. A written handover document from day one, because the founders graduate. A faculty coordinator who signs forms and books rooms, kept informed monthly. Nothing more until the weekly session has run for a semester.**



The mistake that kills most college clubs is not low attendance; it is a founding batch that graduates without a handover. The lessons post covers what I got wrong here first [2].

## How do I get speakers, mentors and judges?

**Invite practitioners with a concrete ask: a topic from their own work, two dates, the audience, the format, what you offer. Start with alumni and engineers in your city, then people who already post about speaking at colleges. Many, including me, speak for free for student communities. Build a record first: a speaker says yes faster to a community with photos of ten past sessions than to one with a plan. Then ask each speaker for the next thing, judging your hackathon, monthly office hours.**


My detailed guide to writing the invitation is a separate page on this site; the short version is six things in one email and a follow-up after five days.


## How do I run a hackathon as a student community?

**Start with a 12-hour internal build day for your own members, then a one-day campus hackathon, then a bigger one with outside teams. Fix the rubric and the timeline before you fix the theme. Recruit judges who have built things and brief them for fifteen minutes. Protect the demo slot: three minutes each, a hard stop, a working projector. Sponsors come after the first successful event, not before. TechVerse Enclave's first hackathon was an afternoon in a classroom; the ones after had partners because the first one had photos.**


The organiser guide with the timeline, rubric and budget lines is on the portfolio [5].

## How do I get sponsors, funding and partner programmes?

**Programmes first, money second. Google Developer Groups on Campus, Microsoft Learn Student Ambassadors, the GitHub Campus Program and Major League Hacking give student communities structure, resources, swag, speakers and credibility, for free [6][7][8][9]. Apply once you have a semester of sessions to show. Local companies sponsor food and prizes for hackathons when you show them last year's photos and this year's plan. College funding follows visible activity, so make the activity visible first.**


## How does a community help your career?

**In every way that a certificate does not. My teammates for three winning hackathons came from it. My first clients came from it. The sessions I ran inside it became the sessions colleges invited me to give. The people I mentored became referrals. Recruiters read "founded a 500-member developer community and mentored 200 students" as leadership evidence no course provides. And teaching every week is the fastest way to actually understand what you are learning.**



## What mistakes do new communities make?

**Spending the first month on a name and a logo. Announcing a big event before running a small session. Founders doing everything and burning out. No handover, so the club dies with a batch. Chasing sponsors before there is anything to sponsor. Measuring the group chat's size instead of the room's. Every one of these I made or watched; the fix for all of them is the weekly session.**



## Can you help our community get started?

**Yes. I run sessions on building and running student communities, speak at inaugurations of new clubs, and connect organisers with the playbook and the templates.** Email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite. Free for student communities.
