# How to structure an LLM project in Python: folder layout, config, prompts as files, evals, and the patterns that survive past the notebook
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-structure-an-llm-project-in-python/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## How should I structure an LLM project in Python?

**As a proper package under `src/`, with separate modules for the model provider, prompts, retrieval, domain logic, API or CLI, and evaluation; typed settings loaded from environment variables; prompts stored as versioned files rather than string literals; Pydantic schemas at every model boundary; a `tests/` folder with a golden set and an `eval` command; and a task runner so `make eval` or `uv run eval` works on any machine. The structure exists so the model can change, the prompts can change and the retrieval can change without touching each other.**


Both production systems I maintain, the RAG platform and the document extraction service, share this shape, and the shape is why a provider swap in one took an afternoon rather than a week [11][12]. My shorter note on the layout is on the portfolio [13]. This page is the full version with the reasons.

> The first time you change models, the structure pays for itself. The second time you change prompts without a test set, you learn why the eval folder exists.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What does the folder layout look like?

**A `src/yourapp/` package with `providers/`, `prompts/`, `retrieval/`, `core/`, `api/` and `eval/` inside it; `tests/` beside `src/` with fixtures and a golden set; `data/` for local indexes and samples, gitignored where large; `scripts/` for one-off jobs; `pyproject.toml`, `Makefile` or task file, `.env.example`, `README.md`. The src layout prevents the common bug of importing the local folder instead of the installed package [1] and forces you to install the project properly.**



## How should I handle configuration and secrets?

**A single typed settings object loaded from environment variables, using Pydantic Settings or equivalent [2]: model names, endpoints, temperature, chunk sizes, feature flags, all with types and defaults. Secrets come from the environment and never from the repository; commit a `.env.example` with the keys and no values [10]. Every module receives the settings object or the specific values it needs; nothing reads `os.environ` directly. This is what lets the same code run on your laptop, in CI and in production.**



## Where should prompts live?

**In files, one per prompt, under `src/app/prompts/`, loaded by a small function that fills placeholders and records which version was used. A prompt is a piece of program logic that happens to be in English; treating it as a string literal buried in a function makes it impossible to diff, review or test. Name files by purpose and version, keep a changelog line at the top, and run the golden set whenever one changes. Templates with explicit placeholders beat f-strings, because the template can be reviewed without the surrounding code.**



## How do I handle model outputs safely?

**Define a Pydantic model for every structured output and parse at the boundary [3]. Use the provider's structured output or tool-calling mode to constrain generation where available [7][8], then still validate, because constraints reduce but do not eliminate malformed output. On failure, retry once with the validation error in the prompt, then fall back to a safe default or a human queue. The rest of the codebase receives typed objects and never raw model text.**


DocuLens is built on this rule: a strict schema per document type, validation at the boundary, deterministic rules afterwards, and a review queue for anything that fails [12]. It is the difference between a demo and a system a finance team trusts.


## How do I set up evaluation in the project?

**A `golden/` folder with labelled cases as JSON or JSONL: input, expected output or expected properties, tags. An `eval` module that runs every case through the real pipeline, computes metrics, retrieval recall, format validity, faithfulness judged by a model or rules, latency, cost, and writes a report. A command, `make eval` or `uv run eval`, that prints the score and exits non-zero if it drops below a threshold. Run it in CI on every prompt or retrieval change. Twenty cases is enough to start; grow it from production failures.**



## How should I log and trace?

**Structured logs, JSON in production, with a request ID that follows the call through retrieval, generation and validation [9]. Log the prompt version, model name, token counts, latency, retrieved document IDs and validation outcome for every call. Store prompts and outputs for a bounded time, with sensitive data redacted, so a failure report can be reproduced. When a user says the answer was wrong, you should be able to find exactly what the model saw.**


## Which tools should I use for the project itself?

**uv for environments and dependencies, because it is fast and produces a lockfile [4]. Ruff for linting and formatting in one tool [5]. pytest for tests [6]. Pydantic for schemas and settings [2][3]. FastAPI if the app serves HTTP. A Makefile or a task runner with `setup`, `test`, `eval`, `run` and `lint` targets so nobody memorises commands. Pre-commit hooks that run Ruff. Nothing exotic; boring tools mean a new contributor is productive in an hour.**



## How do I package and deploy it?

**A Dockerfile that installs from the lockfile, copies `src/`, and runs the API with a production server. Settings from environment variables, so the same image runs everywhere. Health and readiness endpoints. Indexes and data mounted or fetched at startup, not baked into the image if they change. A CI pipeline that runs lint, tests and evals before building the image. Deployment specifics depend on the host; the structure makes them small.**



## What mistakes make LLM projects unmaintainable?

**Prompts as f-strings scattered through functions. Provider calls made directly from business logic, so a model swap touches everything. Raw model text parsed with regex in five places. No golden set, so every change is a guess. API keys in the repository. A notebook as the only entry point. No request IDs, so failures cannot be traced. Everything in one file called `main.py` at two thousand lines. Each is fixed by one folder on this page.**



## Interview questions on LLM project structure

**Explain how you would structure a RAG application so the model can be swapped. Where do prompts live and how are they versioned? How do you validate outputs? What is in your eval set and when does it run? How do you handle secrets? How would you debug a wrong answer reported by a user? A repository that answers these by its layout is the strongest evidence you can bring.**



## Where should I start?

**Take your current notebook and create the six folders. Move the model call into providers, the prompt into a file, the output into a schema, and five examples into a golden set with an eval command. Two hours, and the project can now change safely.** For a workshop on shipping LLM applications from notebook to production, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.


---

# How to win a hackathon: what judges score, how to pick an idea, and the demo that works live, from three first prizes
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-win-a-hackathon/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is a hackathon?

**A hackathon is a timed competition, usually 24 to 48 hours, sometimes a few weeks online, where small teams build a working prototype that solves a stated problem and then pitch it to judges. The output is a demo, not a plan. The prize is usually cash, credits or an incubation offer, but the lasting value is the project, the repository and the people you built it with.**


The word blends "hack", in the sense of building something quickly, with "marathon". In India the format ranges from a two-day event in a college seminar hall to Smart India Hackathon, the government-run national competition with a months-long process [1]. AI hackathons are the same format with problem statements that expect a model, an agent or a data pipeline in the solution.

I have been on both sides of the table: three first prizes as a builder, at IIT Roorkee, CSJMU Kanpur and MeetKats, a loss I learned more from than any win, and time as a judge and mentor at college events. This page is the version of the talk I give students, with the parts that made the difference between winning and not.

> Every hackathon I won, we solved a smaller problem than the teams we beat. Every hackathon I lost, we tried to solve a bigger one.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## How does a hackathon work?

**Registration opens weeks ahead. Teams form, usually two to five people. On the day, organisers reveal or confirm the problem statements, the timer starts, and teams build. Mentors circulate. At the end, each team submits code and a short deck and gets a few minutes to demo and answer questions. Judges score against a rubric, and prizes follow.**



The single most important line in that timeline is "skeleton with the demo path stubbed end to end" in the first six hours. A team that can click through a fake version of the final demo at hour 6 will have a real one at hour 30. A team that builds features in isolation integrates at hour 33 and demos a crash.

## How do I find and join a hackathon in India?

**Devfolio and Unstop list most Indian college and company hackathons, Major League Hacking lists student events worldwide, Devpost covers global online ones, and Smart India Hackathon runs through colleges via its official portal. Follow the tech clubs of IITs, NITs and nearby colleges on Instagram and LinkedIn, because campus hackathons are announced there first. Register early; good events fill.**



Sources for these listings are the platforms themselves [2][3][4][5]. My recommendation for a first-year: one campus hackathon within a two-hour train ride, in person, before any online one. You learn more from watching thirty teams demo in one room than from a month of tutorials.

### Can a beginner participate in a hackathon?

**Yes, and you should, before you feel ready. Most college hackathons have a beginner track or no prerequisites at all. Join a team where one person can already build a basic web or Python app, take the role that matches what you can do, design, research, presentation, testing, and build the skill of finishing under a deadline. Nobody is judged on their first hackathon; they are judged on their demo.**


## How do I pick a hackathon idea that can win?

**Pick a problem a specific person has, that you can demonstrate end to end in three minutes, where the hardest part is something your team can actually build in the time you have. Start from the problem statement's audience, list five problems that person has, choose the one with the clearest before-and-after, and cut everything that is not on the path from the user's pain to your demo.**


Ideas that won for us, and why:

- **KrishGyan, Changethon 2025 at IIT Roorkee.** Farming advice in the farmer's own voice and language over WhatsApp: pest control, crop health and weather, spoken back, no reading or typing needed. It won because the demo was a voice note in and a voice note out, which any judge could follow, and because the audience was real and underserved [6].
- **BrandHive, Product Genesis at CSJMU Kanpur.** A platform for small businesses and emerging influencers to grow organically without a marketing budget. It won because we showed the whole loop, not a slide of features [7].
- **Annapurna, BYTEBATTLE by MeetKats.** Coordinating surplus food between donors, NGOs and volunteers, with four roles and a verified-impact layer. It won on clarity of roles and a demo that walked one meal from a hotel kitchen to a shelter [8].

And the one that did not: STROT, where we built more and explained less, and a simpler team took the prize [9]. That loss is why every timeline I give now starts with cutting scope.


### What are good AI hackathon project ideas?

**The winning AI ideas apply a model to one narrow workflow with real inputs: voice-first advice for people who do not type, document extraction for a specific paper form, a RAG assistant over one institution's documents, a vision check for one quality problem, an agent that completes one repetitive task end to end. "ChatGPT for X" loses to "this one task, done, with this evidence".**


A frame that produces ideas fast: pick an audience, farmers, first-year students, small shops, clinics, college offices; pick a friction, a form, a queue, a language barrier, a lost document; ask what the AI removes. KrishGyan came out of exactly that frame: farmers, the reading barrier, voice.

## What do hackathon judges actually look for?

**Judges score four things, whatever the rubric calls them: feasibility, does it work and could it exist; innovation, is there a real insight, not just a new coat of paint; practicality, would the stated user actually use it; and problem solving, did you understand the problem before you built. Presentation and teamwork are usually smaller weights. A working demo of a modest idea beats a slide deck of a grand one every time.**



These four criteria, feasibility, innovation, practicality and problem solving, are the ones I put on the screen when I brief a room as a judge, and the ones I wrote about after sitting on panels [10]. The weights change; the questions do not.


### What questions do judges ask in Q&A?

**Who is this for and have you spoken to them? What happens when this fails? How is this different from the existing solution? What would you build next with a month? Which part did you write yourselves versus take from a library? Judges use Q&A to find out whether you understand your own project, so short honest answers beat confident vague ones.**


## How do I pitch a hackathon project?

**In three minutes: thirty seconds on who has the problem and what it costs them, ninety seconds of live demo on the happy path, thirty seconds on how it works with one architecture slide, and thirty seconds on what you would do next and what you are asking for. Say the user's name, not the technology's, in the first sentence. Rehearse it three times with a timer.**



For Smart India Hackathon the format is more formal and the template is prescribed, but the same order inside it wins: problem, demo, how, next. Teams that open with a slide of technologies lose the room in the first fifteen seconds.

### How do I give a demo that works live?

**Freeze your code at least two hours before demos. Rehearse the exact click path three times on the machine you will present from, on the venue Wi-Fi if you can. Seed the data so the demo never depends on a live network call you do not control. Record a backup video of the full path and have it open in a tab. Assign one person to drive and one to talk.**


The demo that failed for us at STROT failed on a live API call over venue Wi-Fi. Every demo since has run on seeded data with a recorded fallback, and none has failed.

## How should a hackathon team be formed?

**Three people with three roles: one who builds the core, one who owns the interface and the data, one who owns the problem, the deck and the pitch and also tests everything. Decide roles before the event, not at hour one. A friend who cannot code but can research users and present is worth more than a fourth developer.**


Every first prize we won was a team of three with those roles. Teams of five spend their first three hours negotiating and their last three merging conflicts.


## What is Smart India Hackathon and how do I crack it?

**Smart India Hackathon is a national competition run by the Ministry of Education's Innovation Cell in which student teams solve problem statements posted by government ministries and industry. Teams register through their college, are shortlisted internally, then compete at the national level. To do well: pick a problem statement whose owner you can reach, build a working prototype early, and make the presentation about the ministry's outcome, not your stack.**


The official portal carries the current year's problem statements, timeline and eligibility, and it changes each cycle, so read it rather than any summary, including this one [1]. What stays constant: the internal college round eliminates most teams, so treat the internal presentation as the real competition, and the national judges are domain experts from the problem's ministry, so the domain matters more than the demo polish.

## Do hackathons help your career or resume?

**Yes, when you turn them into evidence: a public repository with a readable README, a two-minute demo video, and a short write-up of the problem, the decision you made and the result. A line saying "participated in 6 hackathons" does nothing. A line saying "1st prize, Changethon 2025, IIT Roorkee, built a voice-first farming assistant over WhatsApp" with a link does the work of a semester of grades.**


On LinkedIn, add the hackathon under Honours & awards with the issuer and date, and post the demo video the same week; hackathon posts travel further than any other student content, in my experience running a 500-member community. On the resume, one line per win, with the problem and the result, and the repository link.

## What mistakes make teams lose?

**Building for 34 hours and presenting for 2. Choosing a problem to impress rather than to solve. No roles, so everyone builds the same screen. A live demo that depends on Wi-Fi. A deck that opens with the tech stack. Not talking to a single real user. Sleeping zero hours and demoing incoherently. Every one of these is cheaper to avoid than to recover from.**



## What should I do after the hackathon?

**Within a week: clean the repository, write the README, publish the demo video, and post the story. Within a month: decide whether the project deserves users, and if so, ship the smallest real version. Annapurna went from a hackathon prize to a tool people used because we kept the roles that worked and threw away the parts built for the judges.**



## Can I invite a judge or mentor to my college hackathon?

**Yes. Organisers can reach me for judging, mentoring or a session on hackathon strategy before your event, on-site across India or remote. What I need from you is the date, the format, the problem statements if fixed, and the rubric you plan to use, or I will bring the four-criteria one above.**


The details and the invite form are at pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite, and my email is pranjulrathour41@gmail.com. Free for student communities.

# How to write a tech resume as a fresher in India: the one-page format, what to put instead of a skills wall, and a free resume website that beats a PDF
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-write-a-tech-resume-for-freshers-in-india/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## How should a fresher write a tech resume?

**One page. A header with your name, one line describing what you build, and links to email, GitHub and a portfolio, no photo, no objective paragraph. A projects section with three entries, each with the problem, the decision, and a measurable outcome, ahead of education. A short skills line, not a wall. Education below projects, since for a fresher the projects are the evidence and the degree is context. Nothing that needs a second page has earned its place yet.**


I have reviewed enough fresher resumes at hackathons and campus sessions to see the same mistakes repeat: a skills wall with forty items, an objective paragraph nobody reads, and projects buried under a "certifications" section three times its length. This page is the fix, plus the free resume-website option that often works better than the PDF itself [6].

> A resume is not a list of everything you know. It is three pieces of evidence that you can do the job, arranged so a tired recruiter finds them in ten seconds.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What should be at the top of the resume?

**Your name, a phone number, an email you actually check, and three links: GitHub, a portfolio or LinkedIn, and one more if relevant. Under that, one line: what you build and one proof, the same sentence your LinkedIn headline should carry [3]. Not "Computer Science student seeking opportunities". Not a paragraph. One sentence a recruiter can read while scrolling past forty other resumes.**



## What goes in the projects section, and how should it read?

**Three projects, each three lines: the problem in one sentence, the decision or hard part in one sentence, and the outcome in one sentence, ideally with a number. "Built a RAG system over 40 pages of college documents; added a confidence gate after early demos returned wrong answers confidently; recall at 5 improved from 61 percent to 89 percent, measured on a 30-question set." That is one project entry. It proves you can scope, iterate, and measure, in three lines.**



My guide to which projects to choose for this section, and the ones that actually get interviews, is written up separately [7].

## Should I have a skills section, and what should it look like?

**A short line or two, grouped by category, not a wall with progress bars: "Languages: Python, JavaScript. Tools: FastAPI, PostgreSQL, Git, Docker." No percentages, no five-star ratings for how well you know a language, which nobody trusts and which ATS systems ignore anyway. List what you can actually discuss for ten minutes in an interview, and nothing you would freeze on if asked a follow-up question.**




## How do I get past an ATS without gaming it?

**Use plain, standard section headings, Experience, Projects, Education, Skills, so parsing software reads them correctly. Avoid tables, columns, text boxes and graphics that confuse a parser, however good they look to a human eye. Mirror the language of the job posting honestly where it matches what you actually did, a posting that says "REST APIs" should be met with "REST APIs" in your resume if that is what you built, not a synonym. None of this is gaming a system; it is writing clearly enough that both a machine and a human parse the same document correctly.**


## What should education look like for a fresher?

**Degree, institution, graduation year, and a CGPA only if it genuinely helps, one line, below the projects section. Coursework only if a specific course is directly relevant and not implied by the degree itself. No list of every subject studied. A recruiter reading a fresher's resume already expects a degree; the projects section is what differentiates one BCA or B.Tech graduate from another.**


## Should I use a resume website instead of a PDF?

**Both, for different moments. Send a clean one-page PDF when a form or an email asks for a resume, since that is the expected format. Link a simple resume or portfolio website in the header for everyone who wants more, because it can hold live demo links, a longer project write-up, and updates without you re-sending a file [6]. A resume website is not a replacement for the PDF; it is the deeper layer the PDF's links point to.**



## What mistakes do freshers make on tech resumes?

**A two-page resume with a full page of certificates and half a project. An objective paragraph that says nothing a recruiter could not guess. A skills wall claiming expert-level everything. Projects described by technology stack instead of outcome, "Built using React, Node.js, MongoDB" with no sentence on what it did or what was hard. Broken links to private repositories. A resume never updated after the first draft, still listing a project from first year as the newest thing built.**



## Tech resume interview questions

**Not asked directly, but tested by every "walk me through a project" question: can you defend every line on the resume for ten minutes without notes. If a bullet point cannot survive a follow-up question, it should not be on the resume. The strongest resumes are the ones the candidate wrote entirely from memory of what they actually did.**



## Where should I start?

**Cut your current resume to one page tonight: header, three projects in three lines each, a short skills line, education last. Then link a portfolio site from the header.** For a resume and portfolio workshop that turns a semester of projects into an interview-ready one-pager, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# Hybrid search and reranking in RAG: BM25 plus embeddings, reciprocal rank fusion, cross-encoders, and why this pair fixes most bad answers
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/hybrid-search-and-reranking-in-rag/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is hybrid search in RAG?

**Hybrid search runs two retrievers on every query, a keyword retriever such as BM25 and a dense embedding retriever, and merges their ranked results into one list. Keyword search catches exact terms, product codes, names, error numbers and rare words that embeddings blur together. Embedding search catches paraphrases and meaning that share no words with the document. Fusing them gives higher recall than either alone, and the fusion itself can be a dozen lines of code with no tuning.**


Hybrid retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion and a cross-encoder reranker is the core of RAG.NextUpgrad's query path, and it is the part of the platform that moved retrieval recall most on the labelled question set [13]. My shorter notes on each half are on the portfolio [11][12]. This page is the pair together, with the papers and the code.

> Users ask for "error E-4021" as often as they ask "why did my upload fail". Only one of those is a semantic query. Ship both retrievers or you will fail half your users.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour, from building RAG.NextUpgrad</cite>

## Why does vector search alone miss results?

**Because embeddings compress meaning and lose exact strings. A product code, a person's name, an error number, an acronym or a version string carries little meaning to the model, so its vector lands near other codes and names rather than near the exact match. Numbers and negation blur too. Dense retrieval was shown to beat keywords for open-domain questions on average [3], and the average hides exactly the queries that matter most in support, legal and technical corpora.**


## What is BM25, and why is it still used?

**BM25 is a ranking function from classical information retrieval that scores a document for a query by how often the query's terms appear in it, weighted by how rare each term is across the collection and normalised for document length [1]. It needs no training, runs in microseconds over an inverted index, and finds exact terms perfectly. It cannot see that "reset my password" and "credential recovery" are the same request, which is exactly what embeddings are for. Together they cover each other's blind spots.**



Learned sparse models such as SPLADE bring some semantic expansion to the keyword side [6], and late-interaction models such as ColBERT keep per-token vectors to recover exact-term precision on the dense side [5]. Both are worth knowing; BM25 plus a dense model plus fusion remains the practical default.

## What is reciprocal rank fusion?

**Reciprocal rank fusion merges several ranked lists into one by giving each document a score equal to the sum, over every list it appears in, of one divided by a constant plus its rank in that list. Documents ranked high in either list rise; documents ranked high in both rise most. The constant, usually 60, dampens the influence of top ranks. It needs no score normalisation, because it uses ranks not scores, and Cormack, Clarke and Buettcher showed it beating more complex fusion methods [2].**


```python
def reciprocal_rank_fusion(*ranked_lists: list[str], k: int = 60) -> list[str]:
    scores: dict[str, float] = {}
    for ranked in ranked_lists:
        for rank, doc_id in enumerate(ranked, start=1):
            scores[doc_id] = scores.get(doc_id, 0.0) + 1.0 / (k + rank)
    return sorted(scores, key=scores.get, reverse=True)

fused = reciprocal_rank_fusion(dense_top_40, bm25_top_40)[:30]   # then rerank these
```

That function is in RAG.NextUpgrad almost exactly as written, because the paper's simplicity is the point: no learned weights, no score scales to reconcile, nothing to retune when you swap an embedding model [13].

## What is reranking, and why not just retrieve more?

**A reranker is a model that reads the question and a candidate passage together and outputs a relevance score. Retrievers compare a query vector with passage vectors that were computed separately, for speed; a cross-encoder looks at the pair jointly, which is far more accurate but too slow to run over the whole corpus. So you retrieve wide with the fast methods, thirty to fifty candidates, and rerank narrow, to the best three to eight. Retrieving more without reranking sends noise to the model, and models use long contexts unevenly [8].**


Passage reranking with BERT-style cross-encoders was introduced by Nogueira and Cho and remains the recipe [4]; Sentence Transformers publishes pretrained rerankers you can run on a CPU for small candidate sets [10].


## How do I choose k at each stage?

**Measure recall at each boundary on a labelled question set. Retrieve enough from each retriever that recall at the fusion output is above ninety percent; forty each is a common starting point. Fuse and keep enough that the reranker sees every plausible passage, twenty to fifty. Rerank down to what the model needs, three to eight, and check recall at that k is still above eighty-five. If recall drops sharply at the rerank step, the reranker is wrong for your domain; if it drops at fusion, one retriever is starving the other.**




## How much does hybrid search and reranking improve results?

**On the labelled sets I have worked with, fusion raised recall at thirty over either retriever alone, and the reranker raised recall at five without touching recall at thirty, which is exactly what each is supposed to do. Public benchmarks such as BEIR show dense models varying widely across domains and BM25 remaining a hard baseline on several [7], which is the research version of the same lesson. Your gain depends on your queries: corpora heavy in codes, names and numbers gain most from BM25; corpora of prose gain most from the reranker.**



## How do I implement hybrid search?

**Keep a keyword index alongside the vector index: Postgres full-text search or a BM25 library over the same chunks [9]; Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Qdrant, Weaviate and others also offer sparse or hybrid support. At query time, run both, fuse with the function above, rerank with a cross-encoder from Sentence Transformers or a hosted reranking API [10], and send the top few to the model. The whole path is a few hundred lines; the design decisions are the k values and the reranker choice.**



## When is hybrid search not worth it?

**Rarely, but there are cases. A tiny corpus where everything fits in the prompt does not need retrieval at all. A corpus of pure prose with no codes or names, where the reranker alone recovers what dense misses. A latency budget so tight that even microseconds matter, which is unusual. In every other case I have seen, the cost of a second retriever is small and the recall gain on exact-term queries is large. Default to hybrid and let your measurements argue you out of it.**



## Hybrid search and reranking interview questions

**Explain why embeddings miss exact terms and BM25 misses paraphrase. Explain reciprocal rank fusion and why it needs no normalisation. Explain the difference between a bi-encoder and a cross-encoder and why you cannot rerank the whole corpus. Describe how you would choose k at each stage and measure it. Say when you would use learned sparse or late interaction models. A retrieval system you built and ablated is the best evidence.**




## Where should I start?

**Add BM25 next to your vector search over the same chunks, fuse with the twelve-line function, and measure recall at thirty on twenty real questions before and after. Then add a cross-encoder and measure recall at five. Both changes take an afternoon and usually deliver the largest quality jump the system will ever see.** For a hands-on retrieval session at your college or team, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# Is AI a good career in India? Roles, what hiring actually looks like, what fresher paths exist, and how to get in without an IIT tag
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/is-ai-a-good-career-in-india/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## Is AI a good career in India?

**Yes, if you build things, and the qualifier matters more than the yes. Companies across India are adding AI features to products and hiring engineers who can ship them; the roles pay at or above general software roles at the same level, and the work is genuinely interesting. But entry-level AI hiring demands proof of shipped work earlier than most fields, and a stack of certificates without a deployed project does not get interviews. I got into GenAI work from a BCA programme in Kanpur without a placement cell by building and posting weekly, and that path is open to anyone willing to do the same [9].**


This page is my honest answer to the question students ask me most at campus sessions, with the industry references that back it [1][2][3] and the paths I have watched work and fail. My roadmap for GenAI engineering in India is written up separately [4].

> The question is never whether AI is a good career. It is whether you will be one of the people with something to show when the interview comes.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What AI roles actually exist in India?

**GenAI or AI engineer: builds features on top of models, RAG systems, agents, fine-tuning, evaluation, deployment; the most-hired role for freshers with projects. Machine learning engineer: trains and serves models, more infrastructure and data pipelines. Data scientist: analysis, experimentation, classical models, business communication. AI product engineer: full-stack developer who integrates AI well. Applied researcher or research engineer: papers and new methods, mostly requires a master's or PhD. Then MLOps, data engineering and annotation or evaluation roles around them. Most openings for freshers are in the first and fourth.**



## How does AI hiring actually work for freshers?

**Campus placements at top colleges bring companies to you; everywhere else, hiring happens through referrals, cold outreach, hackathons, communities and remote applications, and it evaluates what you have built. The interview usually has a coding round, a project deep-dive where you defend your decisions, and a system-design or take-home task such as building a small RAG or extraction pipeline. The project deep-dive is where most candidates fail and where a real shipped project makes you pass [6][7].**



## Do I need an IIT, NIT or IIIT degree?

**For campus placements at those colleges, the tag is the door. For everything else, it is a mild signal that a portfolio overrides. Remote companies, startups and most mid-size product firms evaluate the GitHub, the deployed demo and the interview, and referrals from communities and hackathons open the same doors a tag does [5][10]. I have watched BCA and tier-three B.Tech students get GenAI roles with strong projects and IIT students get rejected with none. The tag saves time; it does not substitute for work.**


## Do I need a master's or PhD for an AI career?

**Not for engineering roles, which are most of the roles. GenAI engineers, ML engineers, AI product engineers and MLOps engineers are hired on demonstrated ability to build. A master's helps for research roles and for some ML engineer roles at large labs, and a PhD is effectively required for research scientist positions. If you want to build products, build products; if you want to publish papers, the degree path is the right one. Choose by what you want to do daily, not by what sounds impressive.**



## What skills do AI jobs in India test for?

**Python, thoroughly. Working with model APIs and structured outputs. Retrieval-augmented generation: chunking, embeddings, hybrid search, reranking, evaluation. Fine-tuning basics with LoRA and when not to fine-tune. Evaluation: how you know it works. Deployment: an API, a container, a free-tier host, logging. Data handling and SQL. Git and a readable repository. Communication: explaining a technical decision to a non-technical person. Not tested for freshers in most roles: deriving backpropagation by hand, training models from scratch, or reciting paper titles.**



## What are the real risks of an AI career?

**Entry-level roles are competitive and demand shipped proof early, so students who only study fall behind students who build. Tools change fast, so the specific framework you learn will be replaced; the skills that persist are evaluation, data handling and systems thinking. Hype produces bad job descriptions and some companies that do not know what they need. Some roles labelled AI are data entry or annotation. And AI tools make junior generalist coding cheaper, which raises the bar for what a junior must bring. None of these is a reason to avoid the field; each is a reason to build rather than collect certificates.**



## What does a first AI job pay in India?

**Enough to be worth it, with wide variance by city, company type and role, and I will not invent numbers here. Startups and remote roles often pay above local service companies for the same skills; product companies pay above both for strong candidates. Compensation rises quickly in the first three years for engineers who ship. The practical advice: research current ranges on public sites for the specific role and city, and negotiate your first offer, because most freshers do not and leave money on the table [8].**


## Which path should I take: placement, remote, startup or freelance?

**Campus placement if your college has good AI hiring; it is the easiest door. Remote roles at foreign startups if you can show shipped work and communicate well; they pay well and evaluate portfolios [5]. Indian startups if you want to learn fast and take ownership early. Freelance and building for local businesses if you want cash flow and real users while you look, which is what I did. Many people combine them: a freelance project becomes a portfolio piece becomes a remote offer.**




## What should my first eighteen months look like?

**Months one to three: Python, one model API, one small deployed app. Months four to six: a RAG system over real documents, measured and deployed; start posting weekly. Months seven to nine: a vision or fine-tuning project with an evaluation; first hackathon. Months ten to twelve: an internship, freelance project or open-source contribution; second hackathon; polish the portfolio. Months thirteen to eighteen: apply widely, interview, iterate on feedback, and keep shipping. My full roadmap with the specific resources is on the portfolio [4].**



## Is AI a good career for non-CS students?

**Yes for engineering roles if you learn to program properly, which takes months of daily practice, not weeks. Domain knowledge is an advantage: a pharmacy student building a prescription reader, a commerce student building an invoice extractor, a biology student building a lab-report assistant each has a project no CS student can match. The route is the same: Python, one API, one deployed project, weekly posts, communities. My sessions for non-CS audiences exist because this route works [7].**



## Where should I start?

**Tonight: install Python, make one API call to a model, and put the script on GitHub with a README. This week: post what you built. Next month: a RAG system over documents you actually have. The career follows from the habit.** For a career session at your college on getting into AI from anywhere in India, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# LoRA vs QLoRA vs full fine-tuning: memory, speed, quality and cost compared, with the settings that matter and how to fine-tune on a free Colab GPU
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/lora-vs-qlora/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## LoRA vs QLoRA vs full fine-tuning: what is the difference?

**Full fine-tuning updates every weight in the model, which needs memory for the weights, their gradients and optimiser states, several times the model's size. LoRA freezes the weights and trains two small low-rank matrices per targeted layer whose product approximates the update, cutting trainable parameters to well under one percent [1]. QLoRA keeps the LoRA adapters but stores the frozen base in 4-bit NormalFloat, so the base itself takes a quarter of the memory [2]. Same adapters, same training loop, radically different memory.**


FineTune Studio, the platform I built in 2026, runs QLoRA from the browser precisely because QLoRA is what makes fine-tuning fit on hardware students and small teams actually have [13]. My own run of a 1.7-billion-parameter model in about 3.2 GB of VRAM is the concrete number behind this page, and the longer comparison notes are on the portfolio [11][12].

> Full fine-tuning is a decision about hardware. LoRA is a decision about speed. QLoRA is the decision that lets you start today.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour, from building FineTune Studio</cite>

## How much memory does each method need?

**Rough orders of magnitude for a fine-tuning run, before activations: full fine-tuning needs about 16 bytes per parameter with a standard optimiser, so a 7B model needs over 100 GB. LoRA holds the base in 16-bit, 2 bytes per parameter, plus small adapters and their optimiser state, so 7B is about 16 to 20 GB. QLoRA holds the base in 4-bit, about half a byte per parameter, so 7B is about 6 to 10 GB with activations at moderate sequence lengths. These move with sequence length, batch size and gradient checkpointing.**



These are planning numbers, not promises. The QLoRA paper's headline was a 65B model fine-tuned on a single 48 GB GPU [2]; my VRAM walkthrough for consumer cards has the measured figures for small models [12].

## How do speed and quality compare?

**Speed: LoRA is fastest per step, because the base runs in 16-bit; QLoRA is slower per step, because 4-bit weights are de-quantised on the fly, though it often wins overall by allowing larger batches on the same GPU; full fine-tuning is slowest and most expensive. Quality: LoRA matches full fine-tuning on most behaviour tasks and lags on tasks needing large capacity changes; Biderman et al. found LoRA learns less but also forgets less [4]. QLoRA matches LoRA closely when adapters target all linear layers [2].**



Lialin et al.'s survey places these among the wider family of parameter-efficient methods [3]; DoRA is a recent refinement that decomposes weights into magnitude and direction and often edges out LoRA at the same rank [5].

## Which should I choose?

**QLoRA if you are on a free Colab GPU, a laptop, or any card under 24 GB, or if you want the largest model that fits. LoRA if you have the memory and want faster iteration, for example a 24 GB or larger GPU with a 7B model. Full fine-tuning only with a multi-GPU setup, a large dataset and evidence that adapters fall short on your task. For almost every student and startup project, the answer is QLoRA.**



## What settings actually matter for LoRA and QLoRA?

**Five. Rank, the adapter's inner dimension: 8 to 32 for most tasks, 64 for demanding ones. Alpha, the scaling: equal to rank or twice it; the ratio sets the adapter's effective learning rate. Target modules: all linear layers, attention and feed-forward, unless memory forbids; the QLoRA paper found this mattered more than rank [2]. Learning rate: around 2e-4 for adapters, ten times higher than full fine-tuning. Epochs: one to three on small datasets; more is memorising. Dropout of 0.05 is a fine default.**



## How do I fine-tune on a free Colab GPU?

**Use QLoRA on a 1 to 7B instruct model with sequence length trimmed to your data, gradient checkpointing, a small per-device batch with accumulation, and either PEFT plus TRL or Unsloth, which cuts memory and time further [6][7][9]. Save adapter checkpoints to Drive or the Hub every few hundred steps because sessions end. A 7B QLoRA run at short sequence lengths fits a free T4; a 1 to 3B run leaves headroom [10].**


```python
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, BitsAndBytesConfig
from peft import LoraConfig
from trl import SFTTrainer, SFTConfig

bnb = BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True, bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4",
                         bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True, bnb_4bit_compute_dtype="bfloat16")
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(BASE, quantization_config=bnb, device_map="auto")
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(BASE)
lora = LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0.05, target_modules="all-linear", task_type="CAUSAL_LM")
cfg = SFTConfig(output_dir="out", num_train_epochs=2, learning_rate=2e-4, per_device_train_batch_size=2,
                gradient_accumulation_steps=8, gradient_checkpointing=True, max_length=1024,
                eval_strategy="steps", eval_steps=50, save_steps=200, logging_steps=10, bf16=True)
SFTTrainer(model=model, args=cfg, train_dataset=train, eval_dataset=val, processing_class=tok, peft_config=lora).train()
```

Argument names change between library versions; check the current PEFT, TRL and bitsandbytes docs before copying [6][7][8]. If memory runs out, in order: shorter max length, batch size 1 with more accumulation, a smaller model.


## What do I do with the adapter after training?

**Either keep it separate and load it on the base at inference, which lets one base serve many adapters, or merge it into the base weights to produce a single model. For QLoRA, merge into a freshly loaded 16-bit base, not the 4-bit one, then quantise the merged model to GGUF, AWQ or GPTQ for serving. Always publish the chat template and the training configuration with the adapter, or nobody, including you next month, can use it correctly.**



## Common LoRA and QLoRA mistakes

**Targeting only attention layers when memory allowed all linear layers. Rank 256 because bigger felt safer. A learning rate copied from full fine-tuning, ten times too low. Ten epochs on five hundred examples. Merging into the 4-bit base. Forgetting the chat template at serving time. Never comparing with the base model. Each is fixed by the checklist above and by the habit FineTune Studio enforces: evaluate base versus tuned side by side before anything ships [13].**



## LoRA and QLoRA interview questions

**Explain what LoRA changes and why it saves memory. Explain what QLoRA adds and the trade-off in speed. Compare quality and forgetting between the three methods. Name the settings that matter and defend a starting configuration. Describe the memory of a 7B run under each method. Explain how to merge and serve a QLoRA adapter correctly. An adapter you trained, with a base-versus-tuned comparison, is the strongest evidence.**




## Where should I start?

**Fine-tune a 1 to 2B instruct model with QLoRA on Colab tonight, on two hundred examples you wrote, and compare it with the base on twenty held-out prompts. Then repeat with LoRA if your GPU allows and compare speed. The difference between the methods is best learned by watching the memory graph.** For a hands-on fine-tuning workshop at your college, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# Mentoring students remotely and internationally: what a mentor actually does, how to find one, and how to run a mentorship program across time zones
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/mentoring-students-remotely-and-internationally/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What does a mentor actually do?

**A mentor asks the question that helps you see your own problem clearly, rather than handing you a ready answer. A teacher covers a syllabus; a manager is responsible for your output; a mentor has no formal stake in the outcome and is there specifically to help you think, usually from having stood where you are standing a few years earlier. The best mentoring I have given or received was rarely advice; it was a question that made the actual problem obvious.**


I have mentored more than two hundred students through TechVerse Enclave and campus sessions in Kanpur, and separately spoken to international student communities remotely, and the two experiences taught me the same core lesson at different speeds: good mentoring is mostly good questions, asked consistently, over time [4].

> A mentor's best sentence is usually a question. The moment you are handing out answers faster than you are asking questions, you have become a lecturer, not a mentor.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## How do I find a mentor without a formal program?

**Ask a specific, well-scoped question publicly or in a direct message to someone whose work you have actually engaged with, not a cold "can you mentor me". People say yes to a real question they can answer in ten minutes far more often than to an open-ended relationship they have to commit to first. A single good exchange, followed by another good question a few weeks later, is how most real mentoring relationships actually start, not a formal ask.**



## What does mentoring look like when it crosses time zones?

**Async-first. A live call every week across a large time-zone gap is where most remote mentoring relationships die, because someone is always awake at 2 a.m. for it. What works instead: a recorded short video or a written update from the mentee on a fixed cadence, a written or recorded response from the mentor within an agreed window, and a live call reserved for when something genuinely needs back-and-forth. Speaking to international student communities taught me this directly: the sessions that stuck were the ones with a recording and a written follow-up, not the live call alone [8].**




## How do I run a student mentorship program, not just one relationship?

**Structure beats enthusiasm at any real scale. Match mentors and mentees by a specific stated goal, not a vague pairing. Set a fixed cadence and a fixed duration, three months, not indefinite, with an explicit renewal decision at the end rather than a silent fade-out. Give mentors a light template for check-ins so quality does not depend entirely on how naturally each one writes. Build in an easy, non-awkward way to end a pairing that is not working, since forcing a bad match to continue helps nobody.**



The community-building side of this, going from five friends to five hundred members, is written up in full separately [5].

## What is the difference between a mentor, a judge, and a speaker?

**A mentor works with you over time on your own goals. A judge evaluates a specific piece of work against a rubric, once. A speaker delivers a session to a room and mostly does not follow up individually afterward. The same person often plays all three roles at different events, and knowing which hat is on matters: a judge who starts mentoring during judging is not being fair to other teams, and a speaker who tries to mentor an entire audience in one session will help nobody well.**



## What mistakes do mentors and mentees make?

**Mentors: answering instead of asking, becoming a free labour source for the mentee's project instead of a thinking partner, and letting a mismatched pairing continue out of politeness. Mentees: asking questions a search engine would answer, expecting a mentor to have all the time a full course would take, and disappearing without closing the loop on advice they were given. Both sides: treating a single good conversation as a permanent relationship without maintaining it.**



## Mentoring interview and program-design questions

**Explain what makes mentoring different from teaching or managing. Describe how you would structure a mentorship program so quality does not depend entirely on individual mentors' natural ability. Explain how you would run a mentoring relationship across a large time-zone gap. Describe how you would end a mismatched pairing without it feeling like a rejection. The strongest answer draws on a specific relationship, not a general theory of mentoring.**



## Where should I start?

**If you want a mentor, send one specific, well-scoped question to someone whose work you have actually engaged with, this week. If you want to mentor others, commit to one person, one cadence, three months, and see it through before you try to scale it into a program.** For a session on building and running a student mentorship program, remote or in person, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# 15 mini AI project ideas you can actually finish in a weekend: small, real, and worth posting about
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/mini-ai-project-ideas-for-weekend-builds/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What makes a good weekend AI project?

**One feature. One real user, even if that user is you or your hostel wing. An API for the hard AI part, so your two days go into the flow and the demo, not into training a model. A visible finish line by Sunday night, however small. The difference between a weekend project and a semester project is not ambition, it is scope: a weekend project answers one question well instead of several questions poorly.**


I keep a running list of ideas exactly like this, because the habit of finishing a small thing every few weekends is what made a bigger project like Annapurna, built for a hackathon and later kept running for real, actually finishable when it mattered.

> A weekend project has failed the moment it needs a second weekend. Cut scope, not sleep.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## Fifteen weekend AI project ideas, with the one hard part named

**Each idea below is scoped to a working version in two days using an existing API or a small open model, with the genuinely hard part called out so you do not discover it on Sunday afternoon.**




## How do I scope one of these to actually fit a weekend?

**Pick the smallest version of the idea that still demos the core value: one input type, one output, no accounts, no settings screen. Use an API for the AI part unless the whole point of the weekend is learning to fine-tune something small. Test on five to ten real examples from your own life, not the cleanest possible sample, before you call it done. If Saturday afternoon shows the idea needs a second weekend, cut a feature rather than extend the deadline.**



## Why bother building something this small?

**Because the habit compounds. A student who ships a small, real thing every few weekends has, within a year, a portfolio of finished work and a public record of building, which is worth more at interview time than one unfinished ambitious project [8]. Small projects are also where you discover the ideas that deserve to become bigger ones; several of the production apps I have built started life as a weekend-scoped idea that turned out to have real legs.**



## What should I do after I finish one?

**Post it the same weekend: a screenshot or a short video, what it does, what was hard, a link if it is deployed. Add it to your portfolio site with the same problem-decision-demo-lesson format as a bigger project [8]. Decide honestly whether it deserves a second weekend of work, most don't, and that is fine, a finished small thing is already a win. Move to the next idea rather than polishing one small project indefinitely.**



## Mini project interview questions

**"Tell me about something you built recently" is answered far better by a finished weekend project with a clear demo than by describing an ambitious unfinished one. Interviewers respond to specificity: what it does, what was hard, what you would change. A stack of small finished things gives you several fresh, specific answers instead of one stale, half-true one.**



## Where should I start?

**Pick one idea from the list, write the one-sentence demo right now, and start this weekend. Two days, one feature, and post it Sunday night.** For a workshop that helps students ship a small AI project in a single sitting, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# Personal branding for developers and CS students: building in public, LinkedIn and GitHub that get you hired, and speaking your way into a reputation
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/personal-branding-for-developers/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is personal branding for a developer, really?

**A public, searchable record of what you have built, explained clearly enough that a stranger can judge it, published on a schedule. That is the whole thing. It is not a logo, a colour palette or a tagline. Recruiters, founders and event organisers search for people who can do a specific thing; a brand is what makes you findable for that thing and credible when found. Mine is "GenAI engineer from Kanpur who ships production AI systems and speaks at colleges", and every post, repository and talk feeds that one sentence.**


I built a developer community to 500-plus members, won three hackathons, spoke at colleges and landed GenAI work without a placement cell, and the thread through all of it was posting what I built every week for years [4][5]. This page is that habit, made explicit, with the profile and channel decisions that mattered.

> Nobody discovers you. They search for something specific and find the person who has been publicly doing it for a year. Be that person for one thing.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What should a developer post about?

**What you built this week, what broke, what you learned, and what you would do differently. A build log with a screenshot beats an announcement. A failure explained beats a success declared. Specific beats general: "I cut RAG latency from 4 seconds to 1.2 by reranking to five passages" is a post; "AI is transforming everything" is noise. Post about the work, the decision and the result, in that order, and tag the tools and people involved when it is true.**



## Which platforms matter for a developer in India?

**LinkedIn, because recruiters, founders, faculty and event organisers in India live there and search there; it is where every speaking and hiring conversation I have had began [1][10]. GitHub, because it is where anyone serious verifies the claims [2]. A personal site, because it is the one place you control where everything resolves [3]. Then one writing home, Dev.to or a blog, for longer pieces [11]. X, Instagram and others are optional amplifiers. Two platforms done consistently beat six done occasionally.**



## How should a CS student set up LinkedIn?

**Headline: what you do and one proof, not your college and year. Banner: a photo from a session, a demo or a hackathon, not a stock image. About: five lines, first person, what you build, one result, what you are open to, how to reach you. Featured: three projects with demo links. Experience: projects and communities count; write them as outcomes. Post weekly. Comment substantively on ten posts a week in your field, because comments are how people without followers get seen.**


My longer guides to LinkedIn for students and to what recruiters actually search for are on the portfolio [6][10]. The single highest-leverage change most students can make in ten minutes: replace "Student at X College" in the headline with what you build.

## How should a developer set up GitHub?

**A profile README with your one sentence, your city, and three links. Five pinned repositories, each with a README that has the problem in one sentence, a screenshot or demo link, how to run it, and what you would do next. Steady commits over weeks rather than one upload per project. Archive tutorial clones. Recruiters spend under two minutes; those minutes should land on finished things with clear explanations.**


The GitHub note, with the README template I use, is written up separately [7].


## How do I write technical posts without a following?

**Start with what you just learned, because a beginner explaining a concept to last-month's self is the most useful writer for the many people at that stage. Structure: the problem, what you tried, what worked, what you would tell someone starting. Include one screenshot or code block. Publish on Dev.to or your blog and post a three-line summary with the link on LinkedIn. Nobody reads the first ten; the eleventh gets found by search, and search does not care about followers.**


My notes on writing a first technical post, and why this site exists as a search-first project rather than a follower-first one, are on the portfolio [8].

## How do I turn projects into talks and a speaker brand?

**Every shipped project is a talk waiting for a room. Offer your college club a session on what you built, with a live demo, then post the photos. Two or three sessions become a page listing the talks you offer, and that page is what organisers book from. Judging a hackathon after mentoring at one adds a second credential. Within a year, invitations arrive with the posts, because organisers search LinkedIn for people who have visibly done sessions before.**



The speaker-brand version of this, with what changed after my first campus sessions, is written up separately [9].

## How do I stay consistent without it eating my week?

**Reuse and schedule. One project produces a post, a demo video, a carousel, a talk and a blog piece; write once, cut five ways. Batch: one afternoon a month to draft four posts, scheduled weekly. Keep a running notes file of things that broke and lessons learned, so posts are extracts, not blank pages. Automate what can be automated, publishing and cross-posting, and keep the writing human. My own posting runs on a pipeline I built for exactly this, so the habit survives busy months.**



## What mistakes do students make with personal branding?

**Posting certificates instead of projects. Announcing instead of showing. Chasing virality with hot takes. Six platforms, none consistent. A LinkedIn headline that says only the college. Copying influencer formats that do not fit a student. Posting nothing for months and then a flood. Faking expertise, which experts spot instantly and never forget. The fix for all of them is the same weekly build log, in your own words.**




## Personal branding interview questions

**Not asked directly, but present in every interview: "tell me about a project" is easier when you have written about it ten times; "how do you learn" is answered by your posts; "why should we hire you" is answered by a profile the interviewer already read. The brand is the pre-read. Make it accurate.**



## Where should I start today?

**Change your LinkedIn headline to what you build, pin three repositories with real READMEs, and post one honest paragraph about what you shipped this week. Then do it again next week.** For a session at your college on building a developer reputation from a campus nobody has heard of, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# RAG vs fine-tuning vs prompt engineering: which one your problem actually needs, with a decision tree and real costs
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/rag-vs-fine-tuning/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## RAG vs fine-tuning: what is the difference?

**RAG, retrieval-augmented generation, changes what the model reads: at answer time it retrieves passages from your documents and answers from them, with citations. Fine-tuning changes what the model is: it trains the weights on your examples so the model's behaviour, style, format or skill shifts permanently. RAG is for knowledge the model lacks or that changes. Fine-tuning is for behaviour no prompt can produce. They solve different problems, and the most common mistake is using one for the other's job.**


I built both kinds of system in the same six months of 2026: RAG.NextUpgrad, a production retrieval platform with hybrid search, reranking and a confidence gate [9], and FineTune Studio, a QLoRA fine-tuning platform with live telemetry and base-versus-tuned evaluation [10]. Clients asked me the same question about both, and this page is the answer I now give before writing any code.

> Knowledge or behaviour? Answer that in one word and you have chosen your architecture. Everything after is engineering.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## When should I use RAG?

**When the answer depends on information the model does not have: your documents, your database, anything after its training cutoff, anything private. When answers must cite their source. When content changes often, because re-indexing a document takes seconds while retraining takes hours. When different users may see different documents, because retrieval can filter by permission and a model's weights cannot. When you need to ship this week, because a RAG prototype is an afternoon.**


Lewis et al. introduced the pattern for knowledge-intensive tasks precisely because a model's parameters are a poor place to store facts that must be exact and current [1]. Ovadia et al. compared knowledge injection by fine-tuning against retrieval directly and found retrieval consistently better at giving models new factual knowledge [3].

## When should I use fine-tuning?

**When the problem is how the model behaves, not what it knows: a consistent voice, a strict output format, a domain's phrasing, a classification or extraction skill the base model does poorly, or a narrow task you want a small, cheap, fast model to do well. When you have hundreds to thousands of clean examples of the right output. When the requirement is stable enough that retraining every month would not be needed. When prompting with examples has been tried and still falls short.**


LoRA made this affordable by training small adapters instead of all weights [2], and LIMA showed how few examples alignment needs when they are clean: a thousand, not a hundred thousand [4]. Both papers point the same way: fine-tuning is a scalpel for behaviour, not a container for facts.

## Where does prompt engineering fit?

**First. A prompt is free to change, takes effect instantly and often solves the problem: a clear task, an output format, a few examples, a rule for the not-enough-information case. Few-shot examples in the prompt were the original demonstration that models can learn a task without training [7]. Every RAG system still needs a well-engineered prompt that says "answer only from these passages and cite them", and every fine-tuning project should start by proving that prompting was insufficient.**



The official prompting guides are free and current; read one before spending on anything else [8].

## RAG vs fine-tuning: side by side

**The comparison, on the dimensions that decide real projects.**



## Can I combine RAG and fine-tuning?

**Yes, and mature systems usually do. RAG supplies the facts; a fine-tune supplies the behaviour: the house voice, a strict answer format, better use of retrieved passages, or a smaller model that follows citation rules reliably. You can also fine-tune the embedding model or the reranker on your own query-passage pairs to improve retrieval itself. Add the fine-tune after the RAG system works and is measured, never before, so you can see what the training actually changed.**



## Can fine-tuning add knowledge to a model?

**Weakly, unreliably and expensively. A model fine-tuned on facts may repeat some of them, but it cannot cite them, it does not know when they changed, and it blends them with prior beliefs. Ovadia et al. found retrieval outperformed fine-tuning for injecting new knowledge, and that repeated exposure to facts was needed for fine-tuning to teach them at all [3]. Luo et al. document the forgetting that aggressive fine-tuning causes [5]. If the fact must be right and traceable, retrieve it.**


This is the expensive mistake I see most: a team fine-tunes a model on their product manual, the manual changes, and the model confidently describes the old version with no way to show where it got it.


## What does each approach cost?

**RAG costs are in retrieval engineering up front, chunking, embeddings, indexing, evaluation, and then per query, because every answer sends retrieved passages as tokens. Fine-tuning costs are up front in the dataset, weeks of a person's time to write and clean examples, plus a few GPU hours that are cheap or free, and then again with every requirement change. Per-query, a fine-tuned small model is cheaper than a large model with a long RAG prompt. Total cost depends on volume and how often things change.**



## What are the failure modes of each?

**RAG fails when retrieval returns the wrong passage, when chunks lose context, when the prompt lets the model ignore the documents, or when passages conflict. Fine-tuning fails when the dataset is inconsistent, when the model overfits and memorises, when it forgets general ability, when the chat template is wrong, or when facts in the training data go stale. Prompting fails when phrasing breaks across model versions and when a task genuinely exceeds the model's ability. Each failure has a specific fix, and none of the fixes is "switch approaches" without measuring first.**



## Which is easier for a beginner or a student project?

**RAG. A retrieval system over documents you know is an afternoon to prototype, runs on a laptop with a free model API or a local model, and teaches chunking, embeddings, prompting, evaluation and hallucination in one project. Fine-tuning is a strong second project once you have a dataset you understand; QLoRA on a small model fits a free GPU. Doing both, and being able to say which problem each solved, is what interviewers want to hear.**



## RAG vs fine-tuning interview questions

**Define both and state the one-line rule. Give an example that needs RAG, one that needs fine-tuning and one that needs both. Explain why fine-tuning is a poor way to add facts, citing forgetting and the inability to cite. Explain how you would prove prompting was insufficient before training. Estimate the cost shape of each. Describe a system you built and which approach it used, and why.**



## Where to go from here

**Build the RAG version first, measure recall on twenty questions, and write down what it cannot do. That list is your fine-tuning specification, if you need one at all.** My longer decision write-up with client examples is on the portfolio [11]. For a session at your college on choosing and building these systems, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.
